## 1 Introduction {#s-1}

### 1.1 Foreword {#s-1-1}

The European Digital Identity Wallet (EUDIW) is a new concept introduced by Regulation (EU) 2024/1183 (eIDAS 2) that enables European citizens, residents and businesses to use a digital identity wallet for identification, authentication, and storage of electronic attestations of attributes. The EUDIW framework introduces novel security, privacy, and interoperability challenges that require clear, well-structured technical requirements.

A Wallet Instance is the software application installed on a Wallet User's device, while a Wallet Unit is the personalised, Wallet User-bound instance of that software which has undergone activation and binding to the Wallet User's cryptographic material and identity. The lifecycle of both the Wallet Instance and the Wallet Unit encompasses multiple stages, from initial installation through to permanent revocation, each presenting distinct security risks and operational requirements.

This specification addresses the lifecycle events of Wallet Instances and Wallet Units. It establishes security requirements that Wallet Providers must implement to ensure that wallet onboarding and lifecycle management processes meet the required security level of as foreseen in the eIDAS, whereby --even if the Wallet Provider strictly speaking is not subject to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2015/1502-- a compromise of a citizen’s wallet will have dire consequences.

This specification was developed to define security requirements to cover the risks that can arise during the lifecycle events of Wallet Instances and Wallet Units. It is intended to serve as a normative basis for conformity assessment of EUDIW solutions with respect to wallet onboarding and lifecycle management processes.

The requirements defined in this specification are risk-based and have been derived from an analysis of applicable legislation, reference frameworks, and threat models relevant to the EUDIW ecosystem. A companion risk register documents the risk analysis underpinning the requirements and is maintained as a separate deliverable.

This specification is intended to be used by Wallet Providers (as a normative framework for implementation) and by Conformity Assessment Bodies (CABs) as a basis for conformity assessment of the Wallet Provider’s implementation.

### 1.2 Scope {#s-1-2}

This specification defines the normative requirements applicable to Wallet Providers for secure onboarding and lifecycle management of Wallet Instances and Wallet Units within the NL EUDI Wallet Certification System. It is a subsidiary requirements specification under NLP-W, the applicable Wallet Provider certification scheme, and the relevant functional and cybersecurity certification requirements for the Wallet Solution.

The specification addresses the provider-operated processes, controls and interfaces by which a Wallet Instance is securely distributed and installed, a Wallet Unit is activated and bound to its Wallet User and cryptographic environment, and the Wallet Unit remains secure, controlled, available and correctly revoked or decommissioned throughout its lifetime.

The scope covers the lifecycle events listed below and the associated operational controls, including security checks, attestation and key management, Wallet User authentication, software maintenance, credential protection, migration and recovery, monitoring, support, uninstallation and revocation:

- Wallet Instance Installation: requirements for the secure distribution, delivery, and installation of Wallet Instance software on Wallet User devices;
- Wallet Unit Activation: requirements for the initialisation, cryptographic binding, and authentication setup that constitute the activation of a Wallet Unit;
- Operational State (Without PID): requirements applicable to a Wallet Unit that is active but has not yet received a Person Identification Data (PID) credential;
- PID Storage and Transition to Valid State: requirements governing the secure storage of a PID and the transition of the Wallet Unit to a fully operational valid state;
- Wallet Unit Management and Maintenance: requirements for ongoing operations including software updates, key rotation, attestation renewal, and account recovery;
- Device Change / Migration: requirements for the secure migration of a Wallet Unit to a new device, including decommissioning of the old device;
- Uninstallation: requirements for the secure removal of a Wallet Instance from a device;
- Revocation (Permanent): requirements for the permanent invalidation of a Wallet Unit.

The object addressed by this specification is the Wallet Provider’s onboarding and lifecyclemanagement service and its controlled interaction with the Wallet Instance, Wallet Unit, WSCA/WSCD, Wallet User, PID Provider and other relevant ecosystem parties. Requirements allocated to the PID Provider remain outside the Wallet Provider’s responsibility. Nevertheless, this specification defines the controls that the Wallet Provider and Wallet Unit shall apply at their side of those interactions because weaknesses or compromise in the wallet environment can invalidate the security assumptions on which PID issuance, storage, presentation and revocation rely.

The following are explicitly out of scope of this specification:

- Wallet Solutions where it is possible that there is more than one Wallet Instance per Wallet Unit active at the same time;
- PID Provider processes, including identity verification (ID proofing) and PID issuance;
- The lifecycle events of the Wallet Solution (build, versioning, solution suspension, solution revocation,…);
- Wallet Solution-level requirements, including organisational, security policy, hardware, software and infrastructure requirements applicable to the Wallet Solution as a whole;
- Lifecycle events of Electronic Attestations of Attributes (EAA) issued by Attestation Service Providers;
- Relying Party requirements;
- Requirements for the interoperability of Wallet Instances across Member States, which are addressed in the Architecture and Reference Framework.

NOTE: This specification does not preclude implementations from imposing additional requirements beyond those specified herein, provided such requirements do not conflict with the provisions of this specification or applicable regulatory requirements.

## 3 Terms & Abbreviations {#s-3}

### 3.1 Terms {#s-3-1}

For the purposes of this specification, the following definitions apply. Terms defined in eIDAS [1] and the Architecture and Reference Framework (ARF) [i.2] are used in accordance with those documents unless otherwise stated.

| Term                                           | Definition                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Wallet Instance                                | The application installed and configured on a Wallet User’s device or environment, which is part of a Wallet Unit and which the Wallet User uses to interact with that Wallet Unit.                                                                                                                        |
| Wallet Unit                                    | A unique configuration of a Wallet Solution that includes one or more Wallet Instances, Wallet Secure Cryptographic Applications and Wallet Secure Cryptographic Devices, provided by a Wallet Provider to an individual Wallet User.                                                                      |
| Wallet Unit Attestation (WUA)                  | A data object, issued by the Wallet Provider, that describes the components of a Wallet Unit and allows their authentication and validation; in this specification it is not one single object but consists of one or more Wallet Instance Attestations and one or more Key Attestations.                  |
| Key Attestation (KA)                           | An attestation issued by the Wallet Provider certifying, for one or more public keys, that the corresponding private keys are generated within and are non-extractable from an identified keystore, and describing the storage type and the security certification of that keystore.                       |
| Wallet Instance Attestation (WIA)              | An attestation issued by the Wallet Provider certifying that a Wallet Instance is a genuine instance of the Wallet Solution, and carrying the information required to determine its revocation status.                                                                                                     |
| List of Trusted Entities (LoTE)                | A list published by the European Commission identifying the entities recognised for a given role in the European Digital Identity framework, together with the trust anchors to be used to authenticate them.                                                                                              |
| Trust Anchor                                   | Public key material, together with the identity of the entity to which it belongs, used as the starting point for validating a certification path.                                                                                                                                                         |
| Wallet Provider                                | A natural or legal person who provides Wallet Solutions.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| Wallet Secure Cryptographic Device (WSCD)      | A tamper-resistant device that provides an environment, linked to and used by the Wallet Secure Cryptographic Application, to protect critical assets and provide cryptographic functions for the secure execution of critical operations.                                                                 |
| Wallet Secure Cryptographic Application (WSCA) | The application component that manages critical assets by being linked to and using the cryptographic and non-cryptographic functions provided by the Wallet Secure Cryptographic Device.                                                                                                                  |
| Person Identification Data (PID)               | A set of data enabling the identity of a natural or legal person to be established, issued by a PID Provider in accordance with eIDAS 2.                                                                                                                                                                   |
| PID Provider                                   | A natural or legal person responsible for issuing and revoking Person Identification Data and for ensuring that the Person Identification Data of a Wallet User is cryptographically bound to a Wallet Unit; typically a Member State authority or body, or a private entity designated by a Member State. |
| Electronic Attestation of Attributes (EAA)     | A set of data in electronic form that allows attributes about a natural or legal person to be authenticated, issued by a (Qualified) Attestation Provider.                                                                                                                                                 |
| Conformity Assessment Body (CAB) | A body that performs conformity assessment activities in accordance with applicable standards and legislation.                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Activation                       | The process by which a Wallet Unit is initialised, configured, and bound to a specific Wallet User, device, and cryptographic key material, rendering it operational.                                                                                                                     |
| Revocation                       | A permanent, irreversible invalidation of a Wallet Unit, after which the Wallet Unit cannot be reinstated.                                                                                                                                                                                |
| Migration                        | The process of transferring the state of a Wallet Unit from one device to another while maintaining continuity of the Wallet User's wallet identity and credentials.                                                                                                                      |
| Key Material                     | Cryptographic keys and associated data generated, stored, and managed within the WSCD for the purpose of securing Wallet Unit operations.                                                                                                                                                 |
| Assurance Level                  | A classification of the degree of confidence in the claimed or asserted identity of a person, expressed as assurance level ‘low’, ‘substantial’ or ‘high’ in accordance with Article 8 of Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 and specified in Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2015/1502. |

## 4 Relation to Resilience & High Assurance {#s-4}

### 4.1 Resilience {#s-4-1}

For the purpose of this specification, resilience refers to the ability of the Wallet onboarding and lifecycle-management processes to maintain the security, integrity and trustworthiness of a Wallet Unit throughout its lifecycle, including when those processes are exposed to attack, compromise, failure or misuse.

Wallet onboarding establishes the initial conditions under which a Wallet Instance becomes a Wallet Unit that can subsequently receive, store and use PID and other attestations. Lifecycle management preserves those conditions as the Wallet Unit moves through the lifecycle events specified in this document, including activation, operational use, maintenance, migration and recovery, uninstallation and revocation.

Resilience therefore depends on more than the security of the Wallet Solution as a product. A Wallet Solution that has been successfully functionally and cybersecurity evaluated can nevertheless cease to provide the intended level of security if the processes through which it is installed, activated, bound, authenticated, maintained, migrated, recovered or revoked can be manipulated or bypassed. The requirements in this specification consequently address the controls necessary to preserve the security properties of the Wallet Unit throughout these processes.

The lifecycle requirements in the following chapters establish defence in depth against attacks on, or misuse of, the individual lifecycle processes. Depending on the lifecycle event, this includes controls intended to:

- prevent counterfeit, modified or otherwise unauthorised Wallet Instances from becoming operational Wallet Units;
- prevent activation or continued operation in an environment that no longer satisfies the required security conditions;
- preserve the binding between the Wallet Instance, Wallet Unit, WSCA/WSCD, protected cryptographic keys and the applicable Wallet User authentication mechanisms;
- prevent cloning, unauthorised transfer or unauthorised use of a Wallet Unit or its cryptographic material;
- preserve the security properties established during initial onboarding when software, cryptographic material, attestations or credentials are updated or renewed;
- ensure that migration, recovery and replacement do not provide a weaker alternative route for establishing control over a Wallet Unit;
- detect conditions indicating that the assumptions underlying the trustworthy operation of a Wallet Unit may no longer hold;
- provide mechanisms for responding to loss, compromise or suspected fraudulent use; and
- ensure that a Wallet Unit that can no longer be trusted can be securely and effectively revoked or decommissioned.

These controls are mutually reinforcing. Resilience is therefore an end-to-end property of the onboarding and lifecycle-management processes rather than the result of any single technical control or lifecycle event. A weakness in one lifecycle process can undermine security properties established by another. For example, strong protection of cryptographic keys during normal operation would not provide the intended protection if an attacker could obtain control through a weaker migration or recovery process, while secure initial installation would not preserve trust if a compromised Wallet Unit could remain operational because revocation was ineffective.

The requirements in the following chapters shall consequently be assessed both individually and in their lifecycle context. The CAB shall evaluate whether the Wallet Provider's implementation maintains the security properties required for the Wallet Unit across the applicable lifecycle transitions and whether alternative, exceptional and recovery paths introduce opportunities to bypass controls applying during the normal lifecycle path.

This concept of resilience is specific to Wallet onboarding and lifecycle management under this specification. It does not refer to the broader organisational cyber-resilience requirements applicable to the Wallet Provider or to requirements governing secure product development and vulnerability management, which are addressed elsewhere within the NL EUDI Wallet Certification System. The purpose of this clause is instead to establish the security rationale connecting the lifecycle requirements that follow: the Wallet Unit should remain trustworthy not only when initially established, but throughout every subsequent lifecycle event that can affect its security or control.

### 4.2 High Assurance {#s-4-2}

The Wallet Provider is not, in its capacity as Wallet Provider, subject to the requirements for assurance levels established by Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2015/1502. In particular, the Wallet Provider does not thereby assume the responsibilities of the PID Provider for identity proofing, identity verification or the issuance of Person Identification Data (PID). These responsibilities remain allocated to the PID Provider in accordance with the applicable regulatory and certification framework.

Nevertheless, the onboarding and lifecycle-management processes performed by the Wallet Provider can have a material impact on the continuing trustworthiness of the digital identity of the Wallet User. Once a PID has been issued to a Wallet Unit following the applicable identity-proofing and issuance processes, the security of that digital identity depends not only on the correctness of the original identity-proofing process, but also on the continued integrity of the Wallet Unit and on the effectiveness of the processes through which that Wallet Unit is activated, maintained, authenticated, migrated, recovered and eventually revoked or decommissioned.

A compromise of these lifecycle processes could undermine the relationship between the verified identity, the Wallet User and the Wallet Unit. For example, an attacker who succeeds in obtaining unauthorised control over a Wallet Unit, its protected cryptographic material or an inadequately secured recovery or migration process could potentially exercise capabilities associated with a digital identity that was originally issued following a correctly performed identity-proofing process. Consequently, the assurance established during PID issuance can be undermined in practice if the Wallet lifecycle processes fail to preserve the security conditions on which subsequent use of that PID relies.

The requirements specified in Chapters 5 to 13 therefore aim to ensure that the Wallet Provider preserves, throughout the applicable lifecycle events, the security properties necessary to protect the relationship between the Wallet User, the Wallet Unit and the digital identity represented by the PID. This includes, as applicable, maintaining the integrity and authenticity of the Wallet Instance and Wallet Unit, protecting cryptographic keys and authentication mechanisms, preserving relevant bindings, preventing unauthorised transfer or takeover, securely managing maintenance and changes, protecting migration and recovery processes, and enabling effective response to loss, compromise and revocation.

In this context, high assurance is not a separate assurance level assigned to the Wallet Provider under CIR (EU) 2015/1502. Rather, it expresses the security objective that Wallet onboarding and lifecycle-management processes shall not introduce weaknesses that could materially undermine the assurance associated with the Wallet User's digital identity. The controls specified in this document are therefore intended to preserve the security conditions necessary for that identity to remain trustworthy throughout the operational lifecycle of the Wallet Unit.

The CAB shall assess the requirements in the following chapters from this perspective. The assessment shall determine whether the Wallet Provider's lifecycle processes adequately protect against circumstances in which compromise, misuse, failure or circumvention of those processes could result in loss of control over the Wallet Unit, unauthorised use of the Wallet User's digital identity, or continued reliance on a Wallet Unit for which the required security conditions can no longer be assured.

## 5 Lifecycle Event: Wallet Instance Installation {#s-5}

### 5.1 Secure Software Distribution and Delivery {#s-5-1}

INST-5.1-01: The Wallet Provider shall sign the Wallet Instance software package using a private key associated with the Wallet Provider’s registered identity in the target distribution platform’s certificate infrastructure, such that the distribution platform or device can verify the signature before permitting installation.

## Guidelines

- Code signing creates a cryptographic link between each published Wallet Instance software package and the Wallet Provider’s registered developer identity. The target platform verifies the signature as part of the installation process and rejects packages whose signatures cannot be validated or do not correspond to the registered developer identity. This requirement applies to every release of the Wallet Instance software, including updates and patches.
- Without code signing, an attacker could substitute a modified Wallet Instance software — for example, via a phishing download link, a compromised mirror, or a malicious app store listing — and users would have no technical means to detect the substitution before installation.
- On Android, code signing is implemented via Android App Signing, where the Wallet Provider registers a signing key or upload key with the distribution channel. On iOS, signing uses an Apple Developer certificate issued to the Wallet Provider. For direct or enterprise distribution outside a platform app store, the platform’s device management infrastructure or managed distribution mechanism provides equivalent signature verification. The specific mechanism depends on the distribution channel used.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the Wallet Provider’s code signing configuration and confirming that the signing key is registered with the Wallet Provider’s identity in the distribution platform. The CAB may also attempt to install a test package signed with an unregistered key and confirm that the target platform refuses installation.

INST-5.1-02: The Wallet Provider shall distribute the Wallet Instance software exclusively through distribution channels that enforce signature verification of the software package as a condition of delivery to the Wallet User’s device.

## Guidelines

- A distribution channel enforces signature verification when the channel itself, or the device’s installation infrastructure, validates the Wallet Provider’s code signature before making the Wallet Instance software available for installation. Official platform app stores enforce this verification as a core part of their delivery infrastructure.
- Without distribution channel controls, a modified or counterfeit Wallet Instance software can reach users through an unauthorized path that bypasses platform-level signature verification, giving users no technical means to detect that the package they install is not the legitimate Wallet Instance software.
- For direct distribution (e.g., a government-operated distribution mechanism for a national wallet), the Wallet Provider documents the integrity enforcement mechanism used by the distribution channel and confirms it is equivalent in effect to platform app

- store enforcement. The list of approved distribution channels and their integrity mechanisms is maintained as part of the Wallet Provider’s security documentation.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the Wallet Provider’s documented distribution channels and confirming that each channel enforces signature verification prior to delivery. The CAB examines whether any unapproved distribution paths exist and whether the Wallet Provider has controls to detect and respond to use of unauthorized channels.

INST-5.1-03: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that the Wallet Instance verifies the integrity of its own software prior to initializing any Wallet Unit functionality, by performing a cryptographic check of the installed package against a reference value established at install time and protected within the device's hardware-backed key store or WSCD.

## Guidelines

- Integrity verification at launch time detects modifications made to the installed software after it was placed on the device — for example by a malware application exploiting root or OS-level access, or by a supply-chain compromise targeting the device's file system after installation.
- Without this control, modifications to the Wallet Instance binary after installation would go undetected and could result in a compromised Wallet Instance operating with the Wallet User's credentials.
- Acceptable approaches include using platform-provided attestation APIs (e.g. Android Key Attestation with Play Integrity, iOS App Attest), hash verification of the application bundle against a signed reference value stored within the WSCD, or OS-level application integrity verification that is enforced prior to any Wallet Unit operation.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the Wallet Provider's technical documentation and confirming that an integrity check is performed at each application launch prior to any Wallet Unit operation. The CAB may corroborate this by inspecting the launch-time integrity-check configuration and, where feasible, by testing that a modified application binary causes the Wallet Instance to refuse to initialise Wallet Unit functionality.

INST-5.1-04: The Wallet Provider shall hold the private signing key used for the Wallet Instance software package in a hardware security module (HSM) that requires multi-person authorisation for each signing operation and that is certified to FIPS 140-3 Level 3, Common Criteria EAL4+, or an equivalent recognised level.

## Guidelines

- Multi-person authorisation means that no single operator can produce a valid signature; at least two distinct authenticated operators are required for each signing event. The HSM enforces this in hardware so that operational compromise of one credential does not lead to unauthorised signing.
- Without this control, an attacker who obtains a single set of operator credentials -- or who exploits a misconfiguration that allows a build server to invoke signing automatically -- can produce signed Wallet Instance software packages that pass downstream signature verification, yielding a malware path indistinguishable from a legitimate release.
- Acceptable approaches include cloud-HSM offerings with quorum-based signing policies, on-premises HSMs with smart-card-based operator authentication, and codesigning services that combine HSM-resident keys with a release-officer approval workflow. The HSM certification level applies to the device itself, not just the cloud platform fronting it.

- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the HSM certificate, the configured signing policy, and the access list for operators authorised to release a signature, and by sampling the audit log to confirm that recent signing events were performed under the multi-person policy.

INST-5.1-05: The Wallet Provider shall record, in a tamper-evident log retained for at least 12 months, every administrative action that modifies the Wallet Instance software package, the code-signing infrastructure, or the configuration of the distribution channel, together with the identity of the operators and the time of the action.

## Guidelines

- A tamper-evident log is one whose entries can be independently shown to be unaltered since their creation, typically by chained hashes, append-only storage with cryptographic anchoring, or write-once media. The log captures both successful and rejected administrative actions.
- Without this control, an insider or an attacker who gains administrative access can modify the build, the signing key configuration, or the distribution settings and subsequently erase evidence of the change, leaving the Wallet Provider unable to detect the compromise during incident response or audit.
- Acceptable approaches include forwarding administrative actions to a central SIEM with cryptographic log integrity protection, using a managed cloud audit-log service with a customer-controlled retention lock, or operating an internal append-only ledger backed by a trusted timestamp authority. Twelve months is a minimum; longer retention may be required by the Wallet Provider's regulatory obligations.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by inspecting the log retention configuration and by sampling logs from the most recent 12 months for a selection of administrative event types to confirm they are retained and complete. The CAB may also review the tamper-evidence design and, where feasible, attempt under controlled conditions to alter a logged entry to confirm that tamper evidence is produced.

INST-5.1-06: The Wallet Provider shall verify, before incorporating any third-party software component into a Wallet Instance software build, that the component's distribution origin is authenticated through a cryptographic signature or hash that traces to a publisher identity declared in the Wallet Provider's approved-supplier list.

## Guidelines

- An approved-supplier list is a controlled register of publishers and components that the Wallet Provider has assessed for security and ongoing maintenance. Verification requires that each component's signature or hash matches a value bound to a publisher in that list, preventing substitution of a similarly named but unverified package.
- Without this control, an attacker who tampers with an upstream component repository, performs a typosquatting attack against a package manager, or compromises a transitive dependency can introduce malicious code into the Wallet Instance software binary. The downstream signature on the Wallet Instance software package will still be technically valid, masking the supply-chain compromise.
- Acceptable approaches include a signed software bill of materials (SBOM) verified during build, integration with a binary repository that enforces signed-publisher policies, vendoring of dependencies into a Wallet Provider-controlled repository, or use of a build system that pins each dependency to a publisher-signed cryptographic hash.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the approved-supplier list, the build configuration that enforces signature or hash verification, and the most recent SBOM produced by a build. Where feasible, the CAB may also attempt to introduce an

unsigned or wrong-hash component into the build to confirm that the build pipeline rejects it.

### 5.2 Device Security Pre-Checks {#s-5-2}

INST-5.2-01: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that the Wallet Instance, at installation and at each subsequent launch, verifies that the operating system version and security patch level of the host device meets the minimum requirements documented by the Wallet Provider, and refuses to activate Wallet Unit functionality on devices that do not meet those requirements.

## Guidelines

- Operating system security patch levels are published by platform vendors on a regular cycle. Devices that are significantly out of date are exposed to known vulnerabilities for which patches exist but have not been applied.
- Without this control, the Wallet Instance could operate on devices running OS versions with known critical vulnerabilities that could be exploited to extract key material or bypass Wallet Unit security controls.
- The Wallet Provider documents the minimum supported OS version and security patch level. The documented minimum is reviewed in response to newly disclosed vulnerabilities. When a new minimum is enforced, Users on non-compliant devices are notified before the change takes effect.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the Wallet Provider's documented minimum OS requirements and the implementation that enforces them, confirming that Wallet Unit functionality is not activated on a device that does not meet those requirements. Where feasible, the CAB may also test the Wallet Instance on such a device and confirm that the application refuses to activate Wallet Unit functionality.

INST-5.2-02: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that the Wallet Instance detects the presence of root access or jailbreak conditions on the host device and, where such conditions are detected, refuses to finalize Wallet Instance Installation.

## Guidelines

- Root access on Android and jailbreak on iOS refer to conditions in which the device operating system's security boundaries have been removed, allowing any process on the device (including malicious applications) to access files and memory belonging to other applications, including the Wallet Instance.
- Without this control, on a rooted or jailbroken device, the file-system sandbox that protects Wallet Instance data from other applications is not enforced. An attacker with root access can directly read the Wallet Instance's data partition and extract keys from software-backed storage.
- The Wallet Provider documents the detection mechanism used and the response applied when root/jailbreak is detected and the mechanism that prevents Wallet Instance Installation.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the Wallet Provider's documented root/jailbreak-detection design and confirming that installation is refused on a rooted (Android) or jailbroken (iOS) device. Where feasible, the CAB may also attempt installation on a rooted or jailbroken test device to confirm that the Wallet Instance installation is impossible.

INST-5.2-03: The Wallet Provider shall implement runtime anti-tampering controls in the Wallet Instance that detect attempts to instrument, hook, or modify the application's execution at runtime.

## Guidelines

- Runtime tampering refers to dynamic instrumentation (e.g. using Frida or similar tools), hooking of system APIs, or memory manipulation applied to a running process. These techniques are used to extract secrets, bypass authentication checks, or intercept cryptographic operations.
- Without runtime protection, an attacker who has obtained physical or logical access to the device can instrument the running Wallet Instance to extract credentials, observe authentication operations, or bypass security controls without modifying the installed binary.
- Acceptable controls include detection of debugger attachment, detection of instrumentation frameworks, integrity checks on critical code sections executed at runtime, and root/jailbreak detection linked to operation refusal.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the Wallet Provider's documented instrumentation-detection design and confirming that the application detects attachment of a dynamic instrumentation framework and refuses to process Wallet Unit operations. Where feasible, the CAB may also attach such a framework to a running test instance and confirm the detection and refusal.

INST-5.2-04: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that the Wallet Unit refuses to finalize Wallet Instance installation when the runtime anti-tampering controls detect an attempt to instrument, hook, or modify the application's execution.

## Guidelines

- Where the runtime anti-tampering controls signal that the application is being instrumented, hooked, or otherwise modified as it runs, installation does not complete: the Wallet Unit stops short of finalising rather than activating on a device where tampering is already present.
- If installation completed despite a detected tampering attempt, the Wallet Unit would be activated inside an environment an attacker already controls, from which credentials and authentication factors could be observed or manipulated from the outset.
- The detection itself is provided by the runtime anti-tampering controls established earlier in this clause; this requirement governs the response to a positive detection, namely halting finalisation of the installation.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the documented anti-tampering controls and confirming that installation performed under an instrumentation or hooking framework the controls detect does not finalise. Where feasible, the CAB may also run Wallet Instance installation under such a framework and confirm that installation does not finalise.

INST-5.2-05: The Wallet Provider shall document and enforce minimum security requirements for devices on which the Wallet Instance may be installed and operated, including at minimum: a screen lock mechanism using a PIN, password, or biometric factor; the availability of a hardware-backed key store; and a supported operating system version receiving security updates from the platform vendor.

## Guidelines

- The minimum security baseline for the host device is a prerequisite for the Wallet Unit's security controls to function as intended. A device without a screen lock or

hardware-backed key store cannot provide the level of physical security required for key material protection.

- Without minimum device requirements, the Wallet Instance could be installed on devices that lack the hardware or OS features required to support the cryptographic operations and access controls on which the Wallet Unit's security model depends.
- The minimum requirements are documented in the Wallet Provider's public terms of use and technical documentation. The Wallet Instance enforces these requirements at installation and at each launch, refusing to activate Wallet Unit functionality on noncompliant devices.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the Wallet Provider's documented minimum device requirements and by confirming that the Wallet Instance refuses to activate Wallet Unit functionality on a test device that does not satisfy them.

INST-5.2-06: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that the Wallet Secure Cryptographic Device used by the Wallet Unit is operated solely under the Wallet Provider’s control, holds a valid security certification appropriate for the applicable Assurance Level prior to its first use by a Wallet Unit, and remains under the Wallet Provider’s exclusive operational control throughout the entire lifetime of the Wallet Unit.

## Guidelines

- In the remote WSCD model, the Wallet Secure Cryptographic Device is not located on the Wallet User’s device but is a cryptographic service operated by the Wallet Provider in a controlled infrastructure environment. The Wallet Provider selects, deploys, and maintains the WSCD independently of any Wallet User’s device, and is therefore in a position to verify and enforce WSCD certification status and operational integrity at all times. This changes the security assurance model: security guarantees derive from the Wallet Provider’s governance of the WSCD rather than from per-device verification at installation time.
- In the remote WSCD model, the Wallet User’s device is not required to host a WSCD and the risk profile therefore does not include the possibility of an uncertified or missing on-device WSCD. The applicable risk is instead that the Wallet Provider fails to maintain the security properties of the remote WSCD — for example by operating an uncertified device or allowing the WSCD to become accessible to parties other than the Wallet Provider. This requirement directly addresses that risk.
- The Wallet Provider’s WSCD certification is documented as part of the conformity assessment evidence for the applicable Assurance Level. The Wallet Provider maintains records of WSCD certification status, including certification expiry dates and renewal obligations, and includes WSCD governance in its ongoing compliance program. Where a WSCD certification approaches expiry, the Wallet Provider initiates recertification or replacement in advance to ensure continuity of conformance.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the Wallet Provider’s documentation of the WSCD used in production, confirming that a valid security certification appropriate for the applicable Assurance Level is current and on record, and verifying that the Wallet Provider’s operational procedures ensure the WSCD remains under their exclusive control. The CAB also confirms that no pathway exists for parties other than the Wallet Provider to operate or access the WSCD.

INST-5.2-07: The Wallet Provider shall implement mechanisms in the Wallet Instance to detect the presence of known malicious applications or anomalous runtime conditions on the host device that could expose Wallet Unit key material or credentials to unauthorised access, and shall, upon detection, prevent Wallet Unit operations involving access to key material until the threat is resolved.

## Guidelines

- Malicious applications on the same device as the Wallet Instance may use overlay attacks, accessibility service abuse, clipboard interception, or keystroke logging to observe or intercept Wallet Unit operations, including attempts to capture the Wallet User’s authentication factors — for example reading the PIN as it is entered, through a window drawn over the PIN-entry screen or through logging of the keystrokes. The presence of such applications creates a threat to the confidentiality of credentials and of the authentication factors that protect them.
- Without threat detection, the Wallet Instance operates in the same environment as known malicious applications without awareness of the risk, relying solely on the OS sandbox. Where sandbox bypass techniques are available or where the malicious application has elevated privileges, this protection may be insufficient.
- Acceptable detection mechanisms include integration with platform-provided security APIs (e.g. Google Play Integrity, Android SafetyNet), detection of known malicious application signatures, monitoring for anomalous accessibility service configurations, and detection of overlay windows drawn over Wallet Unit screens and of input-capture conditions active during authentication-factor entry. The Wallet Provider documents the threats covered, including capture of authentication factors such as the PIN, and the detection mechanism used.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the Wallet Provider's threat detection implementation documentation and confirming that the Wallet Instance responds appropriately to a known malicious application signature or anomalous condition. Where feasible, the CAB may also test the Wallet Instance's behaviour when such a condition is simulated on the test device.

### 5.3 Installation Process Security {#s-5-3}

INST-5.3-01: The Wallet Provider shall distribute the Wallet Instance exclusively through the official app store of the operating system of the Wallet User's device; or, where distribution through alternative channels is necessary, shall implement a mechanism enabling even a Wallet User with low digital savviness to verify the authenticity of the Wallet Instance prior to installation and shall provide the Wallet User with clear instructions for completing that verification.

## Guidelines

- Official app store distribution ensures that the operating system of the Wallet User's device can perform authenticity checks on the Wallet Instance before installation, reducing the risk of distributing a tampered or counterfeit application.
- Where side-loading is unavoidable — for instance, on platforms without an official app store, or for enterprise deployments — the Wallet Provider documents the verification mechanism and ensures that any OS limitations on side-loading are restored after installation.
- Typical verification mechanisms for alternative distribution include code-signing certificate checks, hash verification against a published manifest, or a dedicated authenticity check screen presented by the Wallet Instance on first launch.

- A CAB verifies this requirement by confirming: (i) the primary distribution channel is the official OS app store, or (ii) the alternative distribution mechanism and the verification instructions are documented and validated during certification.

INST-5.3-02: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that the Wallet Instance requests only those device permissions strictly necessary for the functioning of declared Wallet Unit features, and shall present the Wallet User with a plain-language explanation of the purpose of each permission at the time it is requested.

## Guidelines

- Device permissions (such as camera, location, or biometric access) grant the Wallet Instance access to sensitive device resources. Requesting permissions beyond those required for declared functionality constitutes unnecessary data collection and conflicts with data minimisation obligations under GDPR Article 5(1)(c).
- Without this control, the Wallet Instance could accumulate permissions not required for its declared functions, creating unnecessary exposure of Wallet User data and expanding the application's attack surface.
- The set of permissions requested is reviewed and documented during each release cycle. Permission requests that cannot be directly linked to a declared Wallet Unit feature are removed before release. The explanation presented at each permission request is in plain language and accurately describes the specific feature requiring the permission.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the Wallet Provider's permission manifest and confirming that each declared permission is linked to a documented Wallet Unit feature, and by inspecting the installation flow to confirm that permission request screens include clear plain-language explanations. Where feasible, the CAB may also walk the installation flow on a test device to observe these explanations.

INST-5.3-03: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that the Wallet Instance, at the time of installation, operates within an operating system-enforced isolation boundary that prevents co-located applications from accessing, reading, or modifying data stored by the Wallet Instance, including PID credentials, Electronic Attestations of Attributes, cryptographic key material, and any personal data processed by the Wallet Instance.

## Guidelines

- Operating system-enforced isolation takes the form of application sandboxing, confining each application's data to a private storage area inaccessible to other applications at the filesystem level. Mobile operating systems provide this mechanism through mandatory access controls. The Wallet Provider relies on this OS-level mechanism and must not operate on devices where OS-enforced isolation has been circumvented, such as rooted or jailbroken devices.
- Without this control, a malicious application installed on the same device as the Wallet Instance could read PID credentials or other personal data from the Wallet Instance's private storage, access authentication tokens or session state, or interfere with the Wallet Instance's operation. The risk is heightened on devices where the OS-enforced isolation has been removed entirely, enabling any application with elevated privileges to access any other application's data.
- The Wallet Provider may rely on the OS-level sandbox without additional cryptographic file-level isolation above it, provided that the installation-time device integrity assessment confirms that: (i) the OS enforces application sandboxing; (ii) the device shows no indicators of compromise that would undermine sandboxing. Communication between the Wallet Instance and the WSCA is performed through a secure inter-

- process communication channel that does not expose key material to other applications.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the Wallet Provider's technical specification to confirm that the Wallet Instance relies on OS-enforced application sandboxing and that installation is refused on devices where sandboxing cannot be confirmed. Where feasible, the CAB may also attempt to read the Wallet Instance's private data storage from a co-located test application on a compliant device and confirm that access is denied by the OS.

INST-5.3-04: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that the Wallet Instance is shipped with a secure default configuration such that no Wallet Unit functionality is accessible prior to completion of the initial activation process and no personal data is transmitted by the Wallet Instance before the Wallet User has accepted all required privacy disclosures.

## Guidelines

- Secure-by-default configuration means the application's initial state requires active steps (activation, consent) before any functionality involving credentials or personal data is enabled. There is no partial activation path that bypasses security setup.
- Without this control, a partially configured Wallet Instance could expose default credentials, transmit device identifiers, or accept connections before the Wallet User has provided consent.
- The Wallet Provider documents the security configuration baseline applied to all shipped Wallet Instance builds, including network connectivity restrictions, credential access restrictions, and data transmission restrictions enforced prior to activation completion.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the documented pre-activation behaviour of the Wallet Instance and confirming that, before activation is complete, no Wallet Unit functionality is accessible, no sensitive data is transmitted, and the application does not accept connections from external services. Where feasible, the CAB may also test a freshly installed Wallet Instance prior to completing activation to confirm this behaviour.

### 5.4 Wallet User Information and Consent {#s-5-4}

INST-5.4-01: The Wallet Provider shall present the Wallet User, prior to completing installation of the Wallet Instance, with clear and comprehensible information about the nature of the wallet, the categories of personal data processed, the applicable terms and conditions, and the security responsibilities of the Wallet User.

## Guidelines

- The disclosure prior to installation covers the categories of personal data collected and processed during installation and ongoing use (including, for example, device identifiers and biometric data if used for authentication), the applicable terms and conditions of use, the Wallet User's security responsibilities including the obligation to protect access credentials, and any data sharing relationships with PID Providers, Attestation Providers, or other parties. The Wallet User's acceptance of the disclosures is recorded and retained by the Wallet Provider.
- In a scenario where a Wallet User installs a Wallet Instance without receiving adequate information about how the wallet processes personal data, the applicable terms and conditions, or their security responsibilities, the Wallet User could use the wallet in ways that expose them to unauthorised credential presentation or identity theft — for instance, by sharing their authentication credentials or installing the wallet on a

compromised device without understanding the security implications. Absence of adequate disclosure also removes the legal basis for personal data processing under applicable data protection law.

- Disclosure is typically implemented as a mandatory consent screen presented during the installation flow, before the installation can proceed. The privacy notice and terms of service are presented in plain, non-technical language. The implementation can use a multi-step presentation where different categories of disclosure are presented in sequence. All required disclosures are presented before the installation completes — deferred or post-installation disclosure does not satisfy this requirement. Versions in the Wallet User's preferred official language are provided.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the Wallet Provider's documentation to confirm the content of the required disclosures - covering the categories of personal data, terms and conditions, and security responsibilities - and the mechanism for recording Wallet User consent. Where feasible, the CAB may also perform a fresh installation to confirm that all required disclosures are displayed before installation completes and that installation cannot proceed without acknowledgement of them.

INST-5.4-02: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that the Wallet User is presented with the Wallet Provider's terms of service prior to completing installation of the Wallet Instance, that acceptance constitutes an explicit Wallet User action, and that the Wallet Instance is not operable until that acceptance has been recorded.

## Guidelines

- The terms of service set out the obligations of both the Wallet Provider and the Wallet User in relation to the Wallet Unit. Presenting them prior to completion of installation ensures the Wallet User is bound by those terms before any Wallet Unit functionality is available.
- Without this control, the Wallet User may begin using the Wallet Unit without having been informed of the applicable terms, creating uncertainty about the legal basis for the relationship between the Wallet User and the Wallet Provider.
- Acceptance is an explicit action — for example, ticking a checkbox or pressing a dedicated accept button — that is not pre-selected and cannot be bypassed. The Wallet Provider records the date and version of the terms accepted for each Wallet User.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the documented installation flow and confirming that the terms are presented before it completes, that acceptance requires an explicit Wallet User action, and that the Wallet Instance cannot be used if the acceptance step is bypassed. Where feasible, the CAB may also perform a fresh installation to confirm this behaviour.

INST-5.4-03: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that, prior to completing installation of the Wallet Instance, the Wallet User is provided with a clear and complete description of all categories of personal data processed by the Wallet Unit, the purposes for which each category is processed, and the legal basis under Article 6 of the GDPR applicable to each processing activity.

## Guidelines

- Transparency about data processing is required under GDPR Articles 12–14. The disclosure made at installation time constitutes the primary mechanism by which the Wallet User obtains the information required to exercise data subject rights.
- A disclosure that is incomplete, uses technical language without plain-language equivalents, or omits one or more processing activities does not meet the standard for

- transparency. The Wallet User cannot exercise rights in relation to processing they are not informed about.
- The transparency disclosure covers at minimum: authentication data (device binding key, biometric template hash); operational metadata (session logs, transaction history); identifiers binding the Wallet User to the Wallet Provider; and data shared with third-party service providers. Where processing is based on consent, the disclosure must allow the Wallet User to withhold consent for individual activities without losing access to core Wallet Unit functionality.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the data processing disclosure presented during installation and confirming that: all processing activities are described; the purpose and legal basis for each is stated; and the disclosure is presented in plain language prior to completion of installation.

## 6 Lifecycle Event: Wallet Unit Activation {#s-6}

### 6.1 WSCD/WSCA Initialisation {#s-6-1}

ACT-6.1-01: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that all communication between the Wallet Instance (WI) and the Wallet Secure Cryptographic Application (WSCA) during Wallet Unit activation is conducted over a channel that is mutually authenticated and integrity-protected, so that activation data cannot be intercepted, replayed, or tampered with by a third party.

## Guidelines

- The WI-WSCA interface is the internal channel through which the Wallet Instance instructs the WSCA to perform key generation and other cryptographic setup operations. Because this channel is used to establish the foundational security of the Wallet Unit, it must itself be protected against interception and impersonation.
- Mutual authentication prevents a rogue application from impersonating either the Wallet Instance or the WSCA during activation. Integrity protection ensures that instructions and responses cannot be silently modified in transit.
- For remote HSM architectures, a TLS-based channel with certificate-pinned mutual authentication is typical.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the technical specification of the WIWSCA interface and confirming that mutual authentication and integrity protection are documented and implemented for all supported WSCD architecture types.

ACT-6.1-02: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that all private keys attested in a Key Attestation and all private keys of device-bound PIDs and attestations are generated within the Wallet Secure Cryptographic Device (WSCD), and that those private keys are never extracted from the WSCD in the clear at any point during or after activation.

## Guidelines

- Generating keys within the WSCD ensures that the private key is protected by the hardware security boundary of the WSCD from the moment of creation. Keys that are generated outside the WSCD and then imported cannot benefit from the same level of protection.
- The prohibition on extracting private keys in the clear is absolute. If the WSCD supports key export in encrypted form, the resulting protection level must be equivalent to that of the key when stored inside the WSCD.
- For remote WSCD architectures (e.g., HSM), the key generation occurs on the remote device and the private key is never transmitted to the Wallet Instance or the Wallet Provider backend.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the WSCD's certification documentation and confirming that key generation is an on-device operation and that no key extraction path exists in the clear.

ACT-6.1-03: The Wallet Provider shall verify, before signing and issuing a Key Attestation, that the public keys to be included in that Key Attestation correspond to private keys that were generated by and are stored in the WSCA/WSCD described in that attestation, and that those private keys remain under the exclusive control of the Wallet User.

## Guidelines

- By signing a WUA, the Wallet Provider attests to the binding between the public keys in the WUA and the WSCA/WSCD that holds the corresponding private keys. This

verification step is the Wallet Provider's mechanism for ensuring the accuracy of that attestation.

- For remote HSMs, the HSM management interface provides the required assurance.
- Exclusive control by the Wallet User means that no party other than the Wallet User (including the Wallet Provider) can use the private key to perform cryptographic operations. The Wallet Provider must not hold a copy of or escrow the private key.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by examining the key attestation mechanism documented in the Wallet Provider's technical specification and confirming that verification occurs prior to each WUA issuance.

### 6.2 Wallet Instance Attestation and Key Attestation Issuance {#s-6-2}

ACT-6.2-01: The Wallet Provider shall, before issuing a Wallet Instance Attestation, verify that the requesting Wallet Instance is a genuine instance of its Wallet Solution and that the attestation request has not been replayed, forged, or submitted by an unauthorised party.

## Guidelines

- Verifying the authenticity of the Wallet Instance before WUA issuance prevents an attacker from obtaining a WUA for a fake or modified wallet application, which could then be used to fraudulently request PIDs or attestation.
- Replay protection ensures that a previously captured valid WUA request cannot be resubmitted. This is typically achieved through the use of short-lived nonces or challenge-response mechanisms.
- The Wallet Provider's verification method may rely on an app attestation mechanism provided by the OS (e.g., Android Play Integrity API, Apple App Attest), a challengeresponse protocol using the Wallet Instance's signing key, or a combination of both.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the technical design of the WUA issuance protocol and confirming that both app authenticity verification and replay protection mechanisms are implemented and tested.

ACT-6.2-02: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that the Wallet Instance, during Wallet Unit activation, authenticates the Wallet Provider backend before transmitting any device or WSCD information, so that the Wallet Instance can verify it is communicating with the genuine Wallet Provider and not an impostor.

## Guidelines

- Without Wallet Provider authentication, an attacker could set up a rogue backend that collects WSCD characteristics and device data from a Wallet Instance, enabling targeted attacks on the activation process.
- Authentication of the Wallet Provider backend is typically achieved via TLS with server certificate validation against a pinned or well-known trust anchor associated with the Wallet Provider.
- The Wallet Instance must verify the server certificate before the first data transmission. Certificate pinning or HPKP-equivalent mechanisms are recommended in addition to standard PKI validation to reduce the risk of MITM attacks.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the activation protocol specification and confirming that the Wallet Instance performs backend authentication prior to any transmission of device or WSCD data during activation.

ACT-6.2-03: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that each Key Attestation is cryptographically bound to the keystore of the Wallet Unit by including one or more public keys in the Key Attestation whose corresponding private keys are generated by and stored exclusively in the WSCA/WSCD of the Wallet Unit, so that each Key Attestation is tied to a specific, unique WSCD instance.

## Guidelines

- Device binding ensures that a WUA cannot be transferred to or used from a different device or WSCD instance. Combined with key attestation, it allows PID Providers and Attestation Providers to verify that the Wallet Unit they are issuing to is the genuine device-bound unit they expect.
- A WSCA/WSCD generates a dedicated key pair for the WUA at activation. The Wallet Provider attests — by signing the WUA — that the private keys corresponding to the public keys in the WUA are stored in the specific WSCA/WSCD described in that WUA.
- If a Wallet Unit contains both a WSCA/WSCD and one or more keystores, a separate WUA is issued for each. The Wallet Unit internally tracks which PIDs and attestations are bound to which WSCA/WSCD or keystore.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by examining the WUA issuance protocol and confirming that each WUA contains at least one public key with a corresponding private key provably stored in the described WSCA/WSCD.

ACT-6.2-04: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that each Key Attestation contains, at minimum: (a) information describing the storage type and the security certification of the WSCA/WSCD or keystore in which the attested private keys are stored; and (b) one or more public keys corresponding to private keys generated by and stored in that WSCA/WSCD or keystore.

## Guidelines

- The certification information in the WUA (item a) allows PID Providers and Attestation Providers to verify that the WSCA/WSCD complies with the requirements for Level of Assurance High.
- The Wallet Unit identifier (item d) enables PID Providers to request revocation of the Wallet Unit but must be designed so that it cannot be used to correlate the Wallet User's transactions across different PID or attestation providers.
- Where the WSCA/WSCD supports export of private keys in encrypted form, the Wallet Provider shall include this capability as an attribute in the WUA.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by inspecting sample WUAs against the mandatory content list above and confirming compliance with the format specified in [5].

ACT-6.2-05: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that each Wallet Instance Attestation contains, at minimum: (a) information enabling PID Providers and Attestation Providers to check the revocation status of that Wallet Instance Attestation; and (b) a Wallet Unit identifier that does not enable tracking of the Wallet User across transactions.

## Guidelines

- The Wallet Instance Attestation carries the information that describes the Wallet Unit as a whole, while the Key Attestation carries the information that describes the keystore and the keys it protects. Separating the two allows a Wallet Unit to present key-related evidence to a provider without disclosing more about the Wallet Unit than that provider needs.
- Without revocation status information, a PID Provider or Attestation Provider has no means of establishing that the Wallet Unit it is issuing into has already been revoked, so an attacker who retains a revoked Wallet Unit can continue to obtain new

attestations. Without a non-correlatable Wallet Unit identifier, the same value presented to several providers allows those providers to link the transactions of one Wallet User.

- Revocation status information is commonly conveyed as a reference to a status list together with an index into that list. A non-correlatable identifier is commonly obtained by deriving a value that is not reused across attestation batches. The corresponding key-related content is specified in ACT-6.2-04.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by inspecting the content of Wallet Instance Attestations issued in production, by confirming that a revocation status reference is present and resolvable, and by confirming that the Wallet Unit identifier is not reused in a form that permits correlation between providers.

ACT-6.2-06: The Wallet Provider shall sign each Wallet Instance Attestation and each Key Attestation using only cryptographic algorithms included in the ECCG Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms [6].

## Guidelines

- Using only approved cryptographic algorithms ensures that the WUA signature cannot be forged or weakened by cryptographic attacks. The ECCG Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms [6] list is maintained by ENISA and represents the current European consensus on safe algorithm choices.
- Binding the WUA to the specific issuance context prevents replay attacks in which a previously issued WUA is resubmitted to a different PID Provider or Attestation Provider to obtain an unauthorised credential.
- Two context-binding methods are defined in [5]: (1) the Wallet Provider signs a fresh WUA containing the nonce during the issuance process; (2) the Wallet Unit presents a pre-issued WUA alongside a Proof-of-Possession signature over the nonce, using a private key whose public key is attested in the WUA.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the cryptographic algorithm selection documented in the Wallet Provider's security specification and confirming that contextbinding is implemented for all WUA presentations.

ACT-6.2-07: The Wallet Provider shall bind each Key Attestation to the specific issuance context in which it is presented, either by incorporating a nonce provided by the PID Provider or Attestation Provider into the Key Attestation, or by presenting the Key Attestation together with a Proof-of-Possession signed over that nonce using a private key attested in that Key Attestation.

## Guidelines

- Binding a Key Attestation to its issuance context ties that attestation to the specific request it answers, so it cannot be lifted from one issuance exchange and replayed in another. The binding is achieved either by carrying a nonce chosen by the receiving Provider inside the attestation, or by accompanying the attestation with a proof of possession signed over that nonce.
- Without context binding, an attestation captured in one issuance exchange could be replayed to a different Provider or in a later exchange, letting an attacker present a genuine attestation that does not correspond to the request in front of the Provider.
- The two acceptable approaches are those named in the requirement: embedding the Provider-supplied nonce in the Key Attestation, or presenting the attestation together with a proof of possession signed over that nonce using a key the attestation covers. The choice follows the issuance protocol in use.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the WUA issuance protocol design and confirming that a Key Attestation presented in an exchange other than the one it was

issued for is rejected in the absence of the matching nonce or proof of possession. Where feasible, the CAB may also capture a Key Attestation from one issuance exchange and attempt to present it in a different exchange to confirm that the Provider rejects it.

ACT-6.2-08: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that all unique elements of each Wallet Instance Attestation and each Key Attestation — including the attestation identifier used for revocation status checking, the attested public keys, and the Wallet Provider's signature — have a negligible probability of having the same value across all such attestations issued by that Wallet Provider.

## Guidelines

- Uniqueness of WUA elements prevents two distinct Wallet Units from sharing identifiable values that could enable correlation or impersonation.
- Cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generators (CSPRNGs) should be used to generate all randomised fields, including revocation identifiers and salts.
- The uniqueness requirement applies to the entire set of WUAs issued over the lifetime of the Wallet Provider's service, not only to the current deployment.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the WUA generation implementation and confirming that CSPRNGs are used for all unique elements.

ACT-6.2-09: The Wallet Provider shall manage the validity periods of Wallet Instance Attestations and Key Attestations such that a non-revoked Wallet Unit can at all times present a Wallet Instance Attestation and a Key Attestation each with a remaining validity period of at least 31 days, and shall set validity periods taking into account the risk that such an attestation could become a vector for tracking the Wallet User across multiple issuance transactions.

## Guidelines

- PID Providers are required to revoke a PID when the WUA under which it was issued expires. A minimum remaining validity of 31 days is therefore necessary to prevent disruption of PID validity through WUA expiry.
- Longer validity periods reduce the frequency of WUA re-issuance but increase the window during which a compromised WUA could be misused. The Wallet Provider must balance these competing risks in its WUA validity period policy.
- The validity period policy must account for offline usage: a Wallet User who is offline for an extended period must still be able to present a valid WUA when they reconnect.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the WUA validity period policy and confirming that renewal processes are tested to ensure uninterrupted WUA availability.

ACT-6.2-10: The Wallet Provider shall re-issue Wallet Instance Attestations and Key Attestations to a non-revoked Wallet Unit as needed throughout the lifetime of the Wallet Unit, ensuring continuity of the Wallet Unit's ability to receive PIDs and device-bound attestations without requiring re-activation.

## Guidelines

- WUA re-issuance is distinct from Wallet Unit re-activation. Re-issuance updates the WUA (including new public keys and extended validity) while preserving the existing Wallet Unit state, Wallet User account, and enrolled authentication factors.
- The re-issuance process must apply the same security verifications as initial issuance, including verification that the WSCA/WSCD is still available and compliant, and that the Wallet Instance is genuine.
- The Wallet Unit must proactively notify the Wallet Provider when its WUA is approaching expiry so that re-issuance can be completed before the WUA expires.

- A CAB verifies this requirement by confirming that the WUA renewal workflow is documented and tested, and that no degradation in security verification occurs during renewal compared to initial activation.

ACT-6.2-11: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that device binding for all PIDs and devicebound attestations is implemented by having the WSCA/WSCD or keystore generate a dedicated public-private key pair for each PID or device-bound attestation, and by ensuring that the corresponding private key is generated within and remains protected by the WSCA/WSCD or keystore throughout the lifetime of the attestation.

## Guidelines

- A dedicated key pair per attestation cryptographically ties each credential to the specific WSCA/WSCD or keystore from which it was issued. This prevents a private key that was used to bind one credential from being reused to bind a different credential on a different Wallet Unit, which would make the two credentials appear to originate from the same device without actually doing so.
- Without this control, a single shared key pair could be reused across attestations, enabling correlation of a Wallet User's credentials across different providers, or allowing an attacker who recovers one binding private key to forge possession proofs for all credentials on the Wallet Unit.
- Each PID or device-bound attestation issuance flow begins with the WSCA/WSCD generating a fresh key pair. The public key is included in the issuance request together with a proof of possession and, where required, a key attestation signed by the Wallet Provider. The private key never leaves the WSCA/WSCD. This applies equally to initial issuance and to re-issuance.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the issuance protocol documentation for each attestation type and confirming that a new key pair is generated per issuance, by requesting sample issuance transactions and verifying that the public keys differ, and by confirming that the Wallet Provider's WSCA/WSCD architecture prevents key pair reuse across attestation instances.

ACT-6.2-12: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that every public key to which a PID or a device-bound attestation is bound at issuance is a public key attested in a Key Attestation issued to that Wallet Unit.

## Guidelines

- The Key Attestation is the evidence on which a PID Provider or Attestation Provider relies to establish that the key it binds a credential to is protected by a certified keystore under the exclusive control of the Wallet User. A credential bound to a key that no Key Attestation covers leaves that provider without any such evidence.
- Without this constraint, an attacker able to substitute a public key of their own into the issuance request obtains a credential bound to a key held outside the certified keystore, which can then be used from a device the attacker controls while appearing to originate from the legitimate Wallet Unit.
- A conformant implementation generates the binding key pair inside the keystore and includes its public key in the Key Attestation presented with the issuance request. The dedicated key pair per attestation is specified in ACT-6.2-11.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by comparing, for a sample of issuances, the public key in the issued credential against the set of public keys attested in the Key Attestation presented during that issuance, and by reviewing the issuance logic that enforces this correspondence. Where feasible, the CAB may also attempt an issuance with a key that is absent from the Key Attestation to confirm that it is refused.

ACT-6.2-13: The Wallet Provider shall establish and maintain a documented policy governing the issuance of Wallet Instance Attestations and Key Attestations that satisfies the requirements of clauses 6 and 7 of [9].

## Guidelines

- The policy states how the Wallet Provider operates the attestation issuance service: the practices applied, the obligations accepted, the controls in place, and the terms under which the attestations may be relied upon.
- Without a documented and maintained policy there is no declared baseline against which the practices actually applied can be compared, so a gradual degradation of those practices goes unnoticed by the Wallet Provider, by the providers relying on its attestations and by the supervisory body.
- The attestation issuance policy is normally maintained alongside the general policy requirements applicable to the Wallet Provider as a trust service provider set out in [4].
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the attestation issuance policy against clauses 6 and 7 of [9] and by confirming that the version in force corresponds to the practices observed during the assessment.

ACT-6.2-14: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that the revocation-status-maintenance period of each Wallet Instance Attestation and each Key Attestation it issues to a Wallet Unit is at least as long as the longest administrative validity period of any PID or device-bound Electronic Attestation of Attributes issued into that Wallet Unit on the basis of that Wallet Instance Attestation or Key Attestation, and that the revocation status is maintained throughout that period.

## Guidelines

- A PID or device-bound Electronic Attestation of Attributes is bound to keys attested by a Key Attestation and is issued after validation of a Wallet Instance Attestation. A PID Provider or Attestation Provider relies on the revocation status reference of that Wallet Instance Attestation, and of the Key Attestation, to detect revocation of the Wallet Unit for the whole life of the credential it issues, as required by REV-12.2-08.
