- A CAB verifies this requirement by observing, on a test Wallet Unit, that an anchor newly added to a source list becomes available to the Wallet Unit, and by reviewing the distribution mechanism and its integrity protection.

MAINT-9.9-03: The Wallet Provider shall withdraw from every valid Wallet Unit each trust anchor that has been removed from, or invalidated in, a list retrieved under MAINT-9.9-01.

## Guidelines

- Withdrawal is the security-critical direction of trust anchor management: an anchor is removed from a published list precisely because it is no longer to be relied upon.
- Where withdrawal does not happen, a Wallet Unit continues to accept credentials and presentation requests authenticated under a compromised or decommissioned anchor. An attacker in possession of the corresponding private key can impersonate a provider or a relying party for as long as the anchor remains on the device, and the Wallet User has no means of noticing.
- Withdrawal is applied with the same urgency as distribution of new anchors and is not deferred to a periodic full refresh. The Wallet Provider records which Wallet Units have confirmed the withdrawal so that Wallet Units that have not connected can be identified.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by removing an anchor from a source list, confirming on a test Wallet Unit that credentials authenticated under it are subsequently refused, and by reviewing the records of Wallet Units that have not yet confirmed the withdrawal.

MAINT-9.9-04: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that a Wallet Unit accepts only the trust anchors distributed to it by the Wallet Provider under MAINT-9.9-02.

## Guidelines

- The set of anchors on the Wallet Unit is closed and is controlled exclusively by the Wallet Provider. Anchors present in the operating system trust store, or added locally by the Wallet User or by another application, are not used for validating attestations and certificates in the European Digital Identity framework.
- Where the Wallet Unit also relies on the operating system trust store, any party able to add an anchor there — including a Wallet User persuaded to install a configuration profile, or a device management system under an attacker's control — can cause forged provider and relying party credentials to be accepted as genuine.
- A conformant implementation maintains its own anchor store, separate from the operating system trust store, and validates every certification path in this domain exclusively against that store. The corresponding rejection obligation for PID credentials is specified in PID-8.3-02.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by adding an anchor to the operating system trust store of a test device and confirming that material authenticated under that anchor is not accepted by the Wallet Unit.

## 10 Lifecycle Event: Device Change / Migration {#s-10}

NOTE: This clause covers two scenarios. In the first, the source device is still accessible to the Wallet User and the Wallet Unit is migrated to the new device with the source device's participation (clauses 10.1 to 10.6). In the second, the source device is no longer accessible to the Wallet User - for example lost or stolen - and the Wallet Unit is recovered to a new device from a Migration Object without the source device (clause 10.7); that recovery is itself a trigger to revoke the source Wallet Unit.

### 10.1 Migration Initiation and Authorisation {#s-10-1}

MIG-10.1-01: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that migration of a Wallet Unit is initiated solely by the Wallet User from the source Wallet Unit, including where the target Wallet Unit is operated by a different Wallet Provider, and that no authorisation, approval, or notification by the Wallet Provider is required as a precondition for initiating migration.

## Guidelines

- Migration is the act by which the Wallet User transfers the Wallet Unit's state -- the list of PID and attestation credentials, the transaction log, and any non-device-bound attestation data -- from one device to another, by exporting the Migration Object on the source device and importing it on the target device. The Wallet User may target a Wallet Unit operated by the same Wallet Provider or by a different Wallet Provider; this requirement does not differentiate between the two cases.
- Without this control, a Wallet Provider could refuse to permit migration to a different Wallet Solution, or could impose a notification or approval step that operates as a barrier to migration. Either practice undermines the Wallet User's right to data portability and the EUDIW model's requirement that wallet ecosystems be interoperable.
- Acceptable approaches include exposing a migration or export action in the Wallet Unit Wallet User interface that the Wallet User can invoke at any time without contacting the Wallet Provider, ensuring that the Migration Object is automatically maintained so that initiating migration does not require any preparatory step on the Wallet Provider side, and treating any contact with the Wallet Provider as voluntary on the Wallet User's part.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by inspecting the Wallet Unit Wallet User interface for a Wallet User-accessible migration trigger and reviewing the Wallet Provider's documentation for any policy or procedure that would gate Wallet User-initiated migration, confirming that no Wallet-Provider-side authorisation or approval step is required. Where feasible, the CAB may also initiate migration on a test Wallet Unit and confirm that no such authorisation or approval step is encountered.

### 10.2 Secure Data Transfer Mechanisms {#s-10-2}

MIG-10.2-01: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that at all times an updated Migration Object will be available in the storage location selected by the Wallet User.

## Guidelines

- An up-to-date Migration Object is kept available at all times in the storage location the Wallet User chose, so that a current object exists whenever the Wallet User needs to migrate or recover.

- If the stored object were allowed to fall out of date, a Wallet User migrating after a loss would recover a stale state — missing recently added credentials or settings — or find no usable object at all.
- The Wallet Unit refreshes the stored object as the Wallet Unit's contents change, writing it to the Wallet-User-selected location, so that the latest recoverable state is always present.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by changing the contents of a test Wallet Unit and confirming that the Migration Object in the selected storage location is updated to reflect the change.

MIG-10.2-02: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that the Migration Object is stored in external or remote storage only in an encrypted form that protects its confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity, and that only the Wallet User holds the cryptographic material required to decrypt it.

## Guidelines

- The Migration Object is composed entirely of Wallet Instance app-layer data — specifically a transaction log, re-issuance metadata for PIDs and device-bound attestations, and optionally full data for non-device-bound attestations. It contains no private keys, no WSCD-generated secrets, and is unrelated to WSCD operations. Encryption is applied within the Wallet Instance before the Migration Object leaves the device, so the data is never stored in plaintext outside the Wallet User's device.
- A scenario this requirement addresses is one in which the external or remote storage provider — or an attacker who gains access to it — retrieves the Migration Object and reads the transaction history, re-issuance metadata, or non-device-bound attestation data it contains. Exposure of this data reveals the PID and EAA providers the Wallet User is registered with, provider endpoint information, and a chronological record of wallet activity. For users who opted in to non-device-bound attestation storage, the full content of those attestations is also at risk. A storage provider holding multiple users' Migration Objects in plaintext represents a centralised target.
- Password-based cryptography is one acceptable approach, where the Wallet User's chosen password is the sole source of the decryption password and the Wallet Provider has no access to it. An alternative is to derive the encryption key from a secret bound to the Wallet Unit — for example, a key stored within the WSCD — so that only the Wallet Unit can decrypt the Migration Object. In either case, the Wallet Provider holds no decryption password. Confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity protection are achieved together using an authenticated encryption scheme such as AES-GCM. or upon expiry of the migration session window.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by retrieving a stored Migration Object from the external or remote storage location and confirming that it is stored in an encrypted form from which no plaintext data is recoverable without the Wallet User's secret. The CAB additionally reviews the Wallet Provider's documentation to confirm that the decryption key is not stored on or derivable by the Wallet Provider's infrastructure, and that no Wallet Provider-side pathway exists to access the plaintext content of the Migration Object.

MIG-10.2-03: Prior to presenting the Wallet User with the option to finalise migration and revoke the source Wallet Unit, the Wallet Provider shall verify that the target Wallet Unit is in an active state.

## Guidelines

- An active state for the target Wallet Unit requires that: (i) the target Wallet Unit has completed the activation process, including WSCA/WSCD initialisation and WUA

issuance on the new device; (ii) the PID credential has been delivered to and confirmed as validated by the target Wallet Unit, including verification of the issuer signature and the credential binding to the target Wallet Unit’s keys.

- Active state verification is distinct from a check that all attestations have been transferred. The presence and validation of the PID credential on the target Wallet Unit is the criterion; Electronic Attestations of Attributes are not required to be present for the active state check to pass.
- Allowing the source Wallet Unit to be revoked without the target Wallet Unit being in an active state, will bring the Wallet User in a position without any active Wallet Unit with potentially a more complex setup process for obtaining a new active Wallet Unit as there is no source Wallet Unit that can be used to authenticate the Wallet User.
- A CAB verifies MIG-9.2-01 by confirming that: (i) the Wallet Provider does not present the finalisation option until the target Wallet Unit has passed the active state check; (ii) a target Wallet Unit that has not yet received and validated the PID credential does not pass the active state check; (iii) the active state check result is recorded in the migration log.

MIG-10.2-04: The Wallet Provider shall revoke the source Wallet Unit upon the Wallet User’s explicit decision to finalise the migration.

## Guidelines

- The revocation of the source Wallet Unit is triggered by the Wallet User’s explicit decision to finalise migration, not by the Wallet Provider unilaterally. This decision is recorded in the migration log and is available for audit.
- The risk addressed by this requirement is premature or automatic revocation of the source Wallet Unit. If revocation is triggered by any automated step in the migration flow — such as installation of the Wallet Instance on the new device — rather than by the Wallet User's explicit finalisation decision, the Wallet User may find the source Wallet Unit revoked before they intended to abandon it, leaving a gap where neither device has a fully operational Wallet Unit.
- The finalisation decision screen explicitly states that selecting the finalisation action will result in permanent, irreversible revocation of the source Wallet Unit. The screen does not present other migration steps or decisions alongside the finalisation action, to avoid any ambiguity about what the Wallet User is confirming with their action.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the documented migration flow and its logging and confirming that: (1) the finalisation screen describes the revocation consequence in clear terms; (2) revocation is recorded in the migration log with the authenticated Wallet User session timestamp. Where feasible, the CAB may also test the migration flow to confirm this behaviour.

MIG-10.2-05: The Wallet Provider shall not prevent or delay revocation of the source Wallet Unit on the grounds that the Wallet User has not yet requested reissuance of some or all Electronic Attestations of Attributes held in the source Wallet Unit.

## Guidelines

- EAA reissuance requires separate interaction with each Attestation Provider and may not be immediately possible at the time of migration. This requirement prevents the EAA reissuance status from blocking the revocation of the source Wallet Unit once the Wallet User has decided to finalise migration.
- The Wallet Provider presents the Wallet User with an overview of EAA from the source Wallet Unit that have not yet been reissued to the target device, so the Wallet User is informed of follow-up actions required after migration.

- The risk of delaying revocation until all EAA have been reissued on the target device is that the source Wallet Unit remains live for an indeterminate period after the Wallet User has decided to complete migration. An active source Wallet Unit that the Wallet User believes to be decommissioned remains exploitable by a party with physical access to the source device.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the documented finalisation behaviour and confirming that, when a test Wallet Unit has at least one EAA not yet reissued on the target device: (i) the Wallet Provider does not prevent the Wallet User from selecting the finalisation action; (ii) revocation of the source Wallet Unit proceeds upon the Wallet User's finalisation decision regardless of the EAA reissuance status on the target device. Where feasible, the CAB may also attempt to finalise migration in this state and confirm this behaviour.

### 10.3 New Device Security Verification {#s-10-3}

MIG-10.3-01: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that, before completing Wallet Unit reestablishment on the target device, the target device undergoes the same device security assessment as is required during Wallet Instance installation, including verification that the device meets the minimum hardware and software security requirements defined in the Wallet Provider's security policy and that a WSCD meeting the applicable security certification requirements is available on the target device.

## Guidelines

- Wallet Unit re-establishment on a new device is functionally equivalent to a new Wallet Instance installation on that device in terms of the security requirements that must be met before the Wallet Unit is considered established. The security assessment includes device integrity checks, operating system version requirements, and verification that the WSCD available on the target device holds the security certification applicable at Assurance Level High.
- Without this control, a migration could result in a Wallet Unit that operates on a target device that does not meet the security requirements originally verified during installation. An actor who controls the migration process or a Wallet User who migrates to a less secure device could end up with a Wallet Unit on a device that lacks a certified WSCD, runs a compromised operating system, or otherwise does not provide the security baseline required for a valid Wallet Unit at the applicable Assurance Level.
- The device security assessment on the target device mirrors the pre-installation checks defined in the installation lifecycle event. If any check fails on the target device, the migration process does not complete and the Wallet User is informed of the specific check that failed. The source Wallet Unit is not revoked if the target device fails the security assessment, ensuring the Wallet User is not left without a functional Wallet Unit.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the documented migration security criteria and confirming that the migration flow refuses to complete Wallet Unit reestablishment on a target device that fails one or more of the security criteria required during installation - for example, a device with a non-certified WSCD or a device showing indicators of operating system compromise - and that the source Wallet Unit remains active. Where feasible, the CAB may also present such a target device and confirm that re-establishment is refused and the source Wallet Unit remains active.

### 10.4 Wallet Unit Re-establishment on New Device {#s-10-4}

MIG-10.4-01: The Wallet Provider shall issue a new Wallet Instance Attestation and a new Key Attestation for the new device following the same security verification process applied during their initial issuance, including WSCD certification verification and platform attestation.

## Guidelines

- For the new device, the Wallet Provider issues a fresh Wallet Instance Attestation and Key Attestation using the same security verification as the original issuance, including checking the secure cryptographic device's certification and the platform attestation.
- If migration reused the old device's attestations or skipped the verification steps, a new device that does not meet the security requirements could be admitted, or attestations could be bound to hardware whose properties were never checked.
- Issuance for the new device repeats the activation-time verification — securehardware certification and platform attestation — before the new attestations are issued, rather than treating migration as a lightweight transfer.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the documented migration flow and confirming that new attestations are issued only after the same verification steps as initial issuance. Where feasible, the CAB may also perform a migration to a test device and confirm that new attestations are issued only after those same verification steps.

MIG-10.4-02: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that device binding on the new device is established using a key pair newly generated within the WSCD of the new device and that no device-bound private key is transferred from the old device to the new device.

## Guidelines

- Device binding on the new device uses a key pair freshly generated inside that device's secure hardware, and no device-bound private key is copied from the old device to the new one.
- If a device-bound private key were transferred between devices, the key would no longer be confined to a single piece of secure hardware, breaking the guarantee that a bound credential can only be used from the device it was bound to.
- The new device generates its own binding keys within its secure cryptographic hardware, and the migration transfers only data that is not device-bound, with devicebound credentials re-issued against the new keys.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by inspecting a migration and confirming that the new device's binding keys were generated on that device and that no device-bound private key was transferred from the old device.

MIG-10.4-03: The Wallet Provider shall require the Wallet User to establish authentication factors on the target device through a procedure that meets the same security requirements as the initial setup of authentication factors during Wallet Unit activation, prior to the migration process being considered complete.

## Guidelines

- Authentication factors are bound to the device on which they are established and cannot be transferred from the source device to the target device. A fresh authentication factor setup is therefore mandatory on the target device as part of the migration process. This ensures that authentication factors associated with the source device — potentially compromised or observed by an attacker — cannot be used to access the Wallet Unit on the target device.
- The security requirements for authentication factor setup on the target device need to be the same as those applicable during initial Wallet Unit activation, including binding

of the factors to the WSCD and confirmation that the factors are under the exclusive control of the legitimate holder. The security baseline for authentication factor setup on the target device is not lower than that required for initial activation.

- This requirement complements MIG-10.1-01, which requires verification of the Wallet User's identity before migration is authorised. The present requirement addresses the security of the authentication mechanism that will protect the Wallet Unit on the target device after migration has been completed.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the technical specification of the migration flow and confirming that authentication factor setup on the target device is a mandatory, documented step subject to the same security controls as initial activation. The CAB also tests that authentication on the target device uses factors freshly established on that device, and not any credentials transferred from the source device.

### 10.5 Old Device Decommissioning {#s-10-5}

MIG-10.5-01: The Wallet Provider shall point out the dangers to the Wallet User of a valid Wallet Unit that is not under control of the Wallet User and ask the Wallet User if the old Wallet Unit should be revoked.

## Guidelines

- As part of decommissioning, the Wallet Provider explains to the Wallet User the risks of leaving a valid Wallet Unit on a device no longer under their control, and asks whether to revoke the old Wallet Unit.
- A Wallet User unaware of the danger might leave a fully valid Wallet Unit on a device they have sold or replaced, where it could later be used by whoever holds that device.
- The explanation is given in plain terms at the point of migration or decommissioning, and the Wallet User is asked to decide whether to revoke; the actions that follow from that decision are covered by the remaining requirements of this clause.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the documented decommissioning flow and confirming that the risk is explained and that the Wallet User is asked whether to revoke the old Wallet Unit. Where feasible, the CAB may also run the decommissioning flow and confirm that the risk is explained and the Wallet User is asked whether to revoke the old Wallet Unit.

MIG-10.5-02: [CONDITIONAL] If the Wallet User has indicated a need for the old Wallet Unit to be revoked and the old Wallet Unit is managed by the same Wallet Provider, the Wallet Provider shall start the process to revoke the old Wallet Unit.

## Guidelines

- Where the Wallet User asks for the old Wallet Unit to be revoked and it is managed by the same Wallet Provider, the Wallet Provider starts the revocation of that old Wallet Unit.
- If a Wallet User's explicit request to revoke were not acted upon, an old device the Wallet User has deliberately given up would keep a working Wallet Unit, exactly the outcome the Wallet User asked to prevent.
- On the Wallet User's request, the Wallet Provider initiates its revocation process for the old Wallet Unit; the permanent effect and timing of revocation are covered in clause 12.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by requesting revocation of an old Wallet Unit managed by the same Wallet Provider during decommissioning and confirming that revocation is initiated.

MIG-10.5-03: [CONDITIONAL] If the Wallet User has indicated a need for the old Wallet Unit to be revoked and the old Wallet Unit is not managed by the same Wallet Provider, the Wallet Provider shall give the best possible instructions to the Wallet User what actions the Wallet User should undertake in order to get the old Wallet Unit revoked.

## Guidelines

- Where the Wallet User asks for the old Wallet Unit to be revoked but it is managed by a different Wallet Provider, the Wallet Provider gives the Wallet User the best possible instructions on how to get that old Wallet Unit revoked.
- A Wallet User who cannot revoke an old Wallet Unit held at another provider, and receives no guidance, might simply leave it active, so that a device out of their control keeps usable credentials.
- The Wallet Provider cannot revoke a Wallet Unit it does not manage, so it instead directs the Wallet User to the steps and the other provider's channels needed to achieve revocation there.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by requesting revocation of an old Wallet Unit managed by a different provider and confirming that the Wallet User is given actionable instructions on how to obtain that revocation.

MIG-10.5-04: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that all key material held by the WSCD, all PID credentials and Electronic Attestations of Attributes, and all personal data stored by the Wallet Instance are permanently and irrecoverably deleted from the device before the Wallet Instance uninstallation process completes.

## Guidelines

- The scope of data subject to deletion includes all items created or managed by the Wallet Unit: private and secret key material within the WSCD; PID credentials and Electronic Attestations of Attributes in all on-device storage locations, regardless of format; personal profile data associated with the wallet account; transaction data; and any other application data attributable to the Wallet User. Deletion is performed before the uninstallation process completes, not deferred to a later OS-level cleanup.
- A scenario this requirement addresses is one in which the Wallet Instance is removed from the device — for example as part of a device resale, a factory reset circumvention, or an OS reinstallation — but residual credential data, transaction logs, or key material from the previous installation remains recoverable from the device storage. A subsequent Wallet User of the device, or an attacker with forensic access to the storage, could reconstruct the previous Wallet User's identity credentials or transaction history from the undeleted data.
- Deletion of WSCD-bound key material is achieved by issuing the appropriate key deletion command to the WSCD. Deletion of application-layer data is achieved by invoking the OS-level secure deletion capability or by overwriting the data with a secure wipe pattern. Where the Wallet Unit has associated data in remote storage — such as a Migration Object — the uninstallation flow includes a step that prompts the Wallet User to confirm deletion of remote data, or deletes it automatically with Wallet User notification. The Wallet Instance logs the completion of each deletion step.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the Wallet Provider's uninstallation procedure documentation and confirming that it specifies a defined deletion step for each category of stored data. Where a forensic examination is feasible, the CAB may also perform a guided uninstallation of a test Wallet Unit and conduct a forensic examination of the device storage to confirm that no recoverable credential data, key material, or personal data attributable to the wallet remains after uninstallation.

MIG-10.5-05: [CONDITIONAL] If the Wallet User has indicated a need for the old Wallet Unit to be revoked and the old Wallet Unit is managed by the same Wallet Provider, the Wallet Provider shall ensure that that all cryptographic key material and personal data stored in the old Wallet Unit are irrecoverably deleted from the old device and that the Wallet Instance is uninstalled from the old device the next time when the Wallet Instance connects again with the WSCA.

## Guidelines

- Where the Wallet User asks for revocation and the old Wallet Unit is managed by the same Wallet Provider, the Wallet Provider ensures that the old device's key material and personal data are irrecoverably deleted and the Wallet Instance is uninstalled the next time it reconnects to the secure cryptographic application.
- If the old Wallet Unit were revoked in the ecosystem but its data left in place on the device, the personal data and key material would remain recoverable from a device the Wallet User no longer controls.
- Because the old device might be offline at the moment of decommissioning, the deletion and uninstallation are carried out at its next reconnection; verification that deletion completed, and revocation where it does not, are covered in clause 10.6.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by revoking an old Wallet Unit and confirming that, on the old device's next reconnection, its key material and personal data are deleted and the Wallet Instance is uninstalled.

### 10.6 Secure Deletion of Keys and Attestations on Old Device {#s-10-6}

MIG-10.6-01: The Wallet Provider shall verify that the deletion of all cryptographic key material and personal data from the source Wallet Unit has completed, and shall record the outcome of that verification.

## Guidelines

- Deletion is instructed at the end of migration but executed on a device the Wallet Provider does not control. The verification establishes whether the instruction was actually carried out, and the record makes that determination available afterwards.
- Without verification, a source device that acknowledged the instruction but failed to complete it — because it lost connectivity mid-operation, or because the Wallet Instance was terminated — retains key material while the Wallet Provider's records show the migration as cleanly completed.
- Verification normally takes the form of a confirmation returned by the source Wallet Instance after the deletion completes, correlated with the migration record. The deletion obligation itself is specified in clause 10.5.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the documented deletion-confirmation handling and confirming that the recorded verification outcome is marked unconfirmed when the source device is disconnected during deletion. Where feasible, the CAB may also complete a migration on test devices, inspect the recorded verification outcome, and repeat the migration with the source device disconnected during deletion to confirm that the outcome is recorded as unconfirmed.

MIG-10.6-02: [CONDITIONAL] Where the deletion of key material and personal data from the source Wallet Unit has not been confirmed within a period defined and documented by the Wallet Provider, the Wallet Provider shall revoke the source Wallet Unit irrespective of that confirmation.

## Guidelines

- A source device that never reconnects cannot confirm deletion. Revocation after a defined period ensures that an unconfirmed source Wallet Unit does not remain valid indefinitely.
- Where revocation waits for a confirmation that never arrives, a device that was lost, sold, or retained by an attacker keeps a valid Wallet Unit with usable key material, and the migration leaves two live Wallet Units for one Wallet User.
- The defined period is short enough to bound the exposure and long enough to accommodate a Wallet User who simply has not switched the old device on. Revocation of the source Wallet Unit on completion of migration is specified in clause 10.2.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the documented period and confirming that a source Wallet Unit is revoked once the period has elapsed without the source device being reconnected. Where feasible, the CAB may also complete a migration in which the source device is never reconnected and confirm that the source Wallet Unit is revoked once the period has elapsed.

MIG-10.6-03: [CONDITIONAL] Where the deletion of key material and personal data from the source Wallet Unit has been confirmed under MIG-10.6-01, the Wallet Provider shall revoke the source Wallet Unit if it has not already been revoked.

## Guidelines

- MIG-9.6-01 requires the Wallet Provider to verify and record whether deletion on the source device completed. This requirement ties a confirmed deletion outcome directly to revocation of the source Wallet Unit, alongside MIG-10.6-02, which revokes the source Wallet Unit when deletion is not confirmed within a defined period. Between the two, whatever the verification outcome, the source Wallet Unit does not remain valid once its data is gone or once the confirmation period has lapsed.
- Without this requirement, a source Wallet Unit whose deletion is confirmed could still be left in a valid state. A Wallet Unit that presents as valid and recognised after its holder has moved to a new device and its local data is gone is an exploitable inconsistency between the device’s actual state and its ecosystem-visible status, with no offsetting benefit to the Wallet User.
- The condition "if it has not already been revoked" makes the requirement idempotent: where revocation of the source Wallet Unit was already triggered on completion of migration, this requirement is satisfied by that earlier revocation and needs no further action; where the source Wallet Unit instead reached this point through the decommissioning flow of clause 10.5 without an explicit finalisation step, confirmed deletion is itself the trigger for revocation.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the documented decommissioning path in clause 10.5 and confirming that, once deletion on the source device is confirmed, the source Wallet Unit's status changes to revoked without further Wallet User action, and that where the source Wallet Unit was already revoked no conflicting or duplicate revocation attempt is made. Where feasible, the CAB may also complete a migration through the clause 10.5 decommissioning path and confirm this behaviour.

### 10.7 Recovery to a New Device When the Source Device Is Unavailable {#s-10-7}

MIG-10.7-01: [CONDITIONAL] Where the source Wallet Unit is no longer accessible to the Wallet User, the Wallet Provider shall enable the Wallet User to re-establish the Wallet Unit on a new device by restoring a Migration Object, without requiring any participation by the source device.

## Guidelines

- This is the recovery path for a lost, stolen, broken, or otherwise unreachable source device. The Wallet User brings the Migration Object they hold to a new device and reestablishes the Wallet Unit there; nothing is asked of the old device, because it cannot respond. The restore mechanics are those of clause 6.6.
- Without this path, a Wallet User whose only device is gone would be stranded - unable to migrate in the ordinary way (which needs the source device) and left to start over entirely, or worse, with an old Wallet Unit still live on a device now in someone else's hands.
- The recovery reuses the Migration Object restore and re-issuance flow of clause 6.6; because device-bound keys never leave the device that created them, the credentials are re-issued on the new device rather than transferred. Identity re-proofing and revocation of the source unit are covered by the requirements that follow.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the documented recovery flow and confirming that a Wallet Unit can be re-established from a Migration Object with no action by the source device, for instance by inspecting the flow design and, where feasible, by performing a recovery on a new device while the source device is kept offline.

MIG-10.7-02: The Wallet Provider shall require identity proofing at the assurance level applicable to initial PID issuance before any PID credential is re-issued during a recovery performed under this clause.

## Guidelines

- A recovery to a new device re-establishes a strong identity means; it is therefore gated by the same identity proofing as a first issuance, rather than trusting possession of the Migration Object alone.
- If possession of the Migration Object were sufficient, anyone who obtained a copy of it and guessed or learned its password could stand up the Wallet User's identity on a device of their own; requiring full proofing ties the recovery back to the real person.
- The proofing is the same as for initial PID issuance under clause 8. This requirement concerns only the identity check on recovery; the restore of non-device-bound data follows clause 6.6.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the recovery flow and confirming that PID re-issuance is preceded by identity proofing at the initial-issuance assurance level, for instance by inspecting the flow and proofing records and, where feasible, by attempting a recovery without valid proofing and confirming that no PID is re-issued.

MIG-10.7-03: [CONDITIONAL] Where a recovery under this clause is performed and the source Wallet Unit is managed by the same Wallet Provider, the Wallet Provider shall revoke the source Wallet Unit, treating the Wallet User’s assertion that the source device is no longer under their control as the trigger for that revocation.

## Guidelines

- Because a recovery under this clause is undertaken precisely when the source device is out of the Wallet User’s control, a source Wallet Unit managed by the same Wallet

Provider is revoked as part of the recovery rather than left to time out. The Wallet User’s act of recovering to a new device is taken as the signal that the old unit is no longer theirs to use.

- If the source unit were left valid, a lost or stolen device would keep a usable Wallet Unit in the hands of whoever now holds it, at the same time as the Wallet User stands up a new one — exactly the two-live-units exposure the migration controls exist to prevent, but now with the old device outside anyone’s supervision.
- Deletion on the source device cannot be confirmed here because that device is unreachable, so revocation does not wait for the confirmation or the time-out of clause 10.6; the recovery itself is the trigger. Where the source Wallet Unit is managed by a different Wallet Provider, its revocation is handled under the following requirement instead. Revocation follows clause 12.10.612
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the recovery flow and confirming that completing a recovery revokes a source Wallet Unit managed by the same Wallet Provider without waiting for source-device confirmation, for instance by inspecting the flow and revocation records and, where feasible, by performing a recovery and confirming the source unit’s status becomes revoked.

MIG-10.7-04: [CONDITIONAL] Where a recovery under this clause is performed and the source Wallet Unit is managed by a different Wallet Provider, the Wallet Provider shall give the Wallet User the best possible instructions on the actions the Wallet User should undertake in order to get the source Wallet Unit revoked.

## Guidelines

- Where the Wallet User recovers onto a Wallet Unit operated by one Wallet Provider while the lost source Wallet Unit is managed by a different Wallet Provider, the Wallet Provider gives the Wallet User the best possible instructions on how to get that source Wallet Unit revoked. A recovery can cross providers in the same way a migration can, so the source unit is not necessarily one this Wallet Provider can act on directly.
- A Wallet User who cannot revoke a lost Wallet Unit held at another provider, and receives no guidance, might leave it active, so that a device now outside their control keeps usable credentials — the same lost-device exposure, left unresolved because the provider that performed the recovery is not the one that can revoke the source.
- The Wallet Provider cannot revoke a Wallet Unit it does not manage, so it directs the Wallet User to the steps and the other provider’s channels needed to obtain revocation there. This mirrors the decommissioning handling of clause 10.5 where a migration is to a different Wallet Provider. Revocation, once obtained, follows clause 12.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by performing a recovery in which the source Wallet Unit is managed by a different provider and confirming that the Wallet User is given actionable instructions on how to obtain that revocation, for instance by inspecting the recovery flow and the guidance presented to the Wallet User.

MIG-10.7-05: The Wallet Provider shall apply to the re-establishment of the Wallet Unit on the new device under this clause the same new device security verification and reestablishment controls that apply to a migration, as set out in clauses 10.3 and 10.4.

## Guidelines

- A recovery re-establishes the Wallet Unit on a new device just as a migration does, so the same conditions apply before the new Wallet Unit is treated as established: the new device security verification of clause 10.3, and the re-establishment controls of clause 10.4 — a new Wallet Instance Attestation and Key Attestation, device binding on a key pair freshly generated on the new device with no device-bound private key

- carried over, and authentication factors set up on the new device to the standard required at activation.
- If recovery skipped these checks, a Wallet Unit could be re-established on a device that does not meet the installation security baseline, or on attestations and keys never verified against the new hardware — admitting a weaker or attacker-controlled device through the recovery path precisely when the ordinary migration checks are otherwise absent because the source device cannot take part.
- The new device security verification and re-establishment of clauses 10.3 and 10.4 are carried out against the new device during a recovery exactly as during a migration, the only difference being that nothing is expected from the source device. A new device that fails the verification does not complete the recovery; the lost source Wallet Unit is dealt with by the revocation requirements of this clause and by the Wallet User’s own right to seek revocation under clause 12, independently of whether re-establishment on a new device succeeds.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the recovery flow and confirming that the new device security verification and the re-establishment controls of clauses 10.3 and 10.4 are applied before a Wallet Unit is re-established through recovery, for instance by inspecting the recovery flow design and, where feasible, by attempting a recovery onto a device that fails the security verification and confirming that re-establishment does not complete.

## 11 Lifecycle Event: Uninstallation {#s-11}

### 11.1 Wallet User-Initiated Uninstallation {#s-11-1}

UNINST-11.1-01: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that the Wallet Unit requires an explicit confirmation step from the Wallet User before proceeding with uninstallation and presents the Wallet User with a clear statement of the consequences of uninstallation, including the irreversible loss of all key bound credentials stored in the Wallet Unit.

## Guidelines

- Before uninstalling, the Wallet Unit requires the Wallet User to confirm explicitly and shows a clear statement of the consequences, including the irreversible loss of all keybound credentials held in the Wallet Unit.
- Without an explicit, informed confirmation, a Wallet User could uninstall on impulse or by mistake and only afterwards discover that key-bound credentials — which cannot be recovered — were destroyed.
- The consequence statement makes clear which data is lost and that the loss of keybound credentials is irreversible; uninstallation proceeds only after the Wallet User acts on that confirmation step.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by starting uninstallation on a test Wallet Unit and confirming that a consequence statement and an explicit confirmation step are presented before it proceeds.

UNINST-11.1-02: The Wallet Provider shall, prior to completing the Wallet Instance uninstallation process, inform the Wallet User that all PID credentials, attestations and transaction logs stored in the Wallet Unit will be permanently deleted and are not recoverable after uninstallation, and shall require explicit Wallet User confirmation before proceeding.

## Guidelines

- The Wallet User warning is presented at a step within the uninstallation flow that allows the Wallet User to cancel and take alternative action, such as performing a migration or backing up recoverable attestations and transaction logs. A warning shown only after uninstallation has begun does not satisfy this requirement.
- A Wallet User who uninstalls without understanding that key-bound credentials cannot be recovered could destroy their means of identification and have to repeat full issuance for every credential, discovering the loss only when it is irreversible.
- PID credentials bound to the Wallet Unit’s WSCD are cryptographically irrecoverable after uninstallation and WSCD wipe. The Wallet User warning reflects this fact so that the Wallet User can make an informed decision before proceeding.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the uninstallation flow and confirming that a data loss warning with an explicit confirmation step is present, and that cancellation of the confirmation halts the uninstallation process without deleting any credentials.

UNINST-11.1-03: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that, prior to completing the Wallet Instance uninstallation process, an updated Migration Object is available in the storage location selected by the Wallet User, that the Wallet User confirms to still have access to that location and verify that the Wallet User still has knowledge of the Migration Object.

## Guidelines

- Before uninstallation completes, the Wallet Unit checks that an up-to-date Migration Object exists in the Wallet-User-selected storage location, that the Wallet User confirms they still have access to that location, and that the Wallet User still holds the knowledge needed to use the object.
- A Wallet User who uninstalls believing they can recover later could find the Migration Object missing, the storage location no longer accessible, or the decryption knowledge lost — and, with key-bound credentials gone, no way back.
- These checks are performed as a pre-completion gate: the presence of a current object, confirmed access to its location, and retained knowledge of it are each established before the Wallet Unit finishes uninstalling. The handling when a check fails is covered in the following requirement.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by running uninstallation with each check satisfied and confirming completion, and by removing access to the stored object and confirming the check detects it.

UNINST-11.1-04: [CONDITIONAL] If one of the checks in UNINST-11.1-03 is not met, the Wallet Provider shall ensure that Wallet Unit uninstallation only proceeds after renewed confirmation by the Wallet User.

## Guidelines

- Where one of those pre-completion checks is not met, the Wallet Unit only proceeds with uninstallation after the Wallet User has confirmed again, in full knowledge that recovery might not be possible.
- Proceeding automatically when a recovery check has failed would let a Wallet User destroy key-bound credentials with no viable Migration Object, turning a routine uninstallation into permanent, unintended loss.
- A failed check does not silently block or silently proceed; it surfaces to the Wallet User, who gives a renewed confirmation before uninstallation continues.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by forcing one of the recovery checks to fail and confirming that uninstallation halts until the Wallet User provides a renewed confirmation.

### 11.2 Pre-Uninstallation Security Measures {#s-11-2}

UNINST-11.2-01: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that all active sessions and pending transactions within the Wallet Unit are terminated before the uninstallation process begins.

## Guidelines

- All active sessions and any pending transactions in the Wallet Unit are ended before the uninstallation process begins.
- Uninstalling while a presentation or transaction was still in flight could leave a relying party with an incomplete or ambiguous result, or leave partial state behind that complicates clean deletion.
- The Wallet Unit closes open sessions and settles or cancels pending transactions as the first step of uninstallation, so that deletion operates on a quiescent state.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the documented uninstallation behaviour and confirming that an active session or transaction is terminated before deletion

begins. Where feasible, the CAB may also initiate uninstallation while a session or transaction is active and confirm that these are terminated before deletion begins.

UNINST-11.2-02: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that the Wallet Provider backend is notified of the uninstallation event before or upon completion of the uninstallation process, enabling the Wallet Provider to initiate appropriate deregistration or revocation actions.

## Guidelines

- The Wallet Provider backend is told of the uninstallation before or as it completes, so that the Wallet Provider can carry out any needed deregistration or revocation.
- If the backend were never informed, the Wallet Unit could be gone from the device while the ecosystem still treated it as live, leaving its attestations valid and unrevoked after the device-side data was destroyed.
- Notification reaches the backend at or before completion of uninstallation and triggers the Wallet Provider's deregistration or revocation handling; the confirmation seen by the Wallet User is covered later in this clause.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by uninstalling a test Wallet Unit and confirming that the backend receives the uninstallation notification and can act on it.

### 11.3 Data Cleanup and Deletion {#s-11-3}

UNINST-11.3-01: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that all private keys associated with the Wallet Unit, including keys attested in a Key Attestation, credential-binding keys, and Wallet User authentication keys, are irrecoverably deleted from the WSCD and from all application storage locations during uninstallation.

## Guidelines

- During uninstallation, all private keys associated with the Wallet Unit — attested keys, credential-binding keys, and Wallet User authentication keys — are irrecoverably deleted from the secure cryptographic device and from every application storage location.
- Private keys left behind after uninstallation could be recovered from the device by a later holder or a forensic attacker and used to impersonate the Wallet User or present their credentials.
- Deletion issues the key-destruction operations to the secure cryptographic device and clears any application-layer key storage, covering every category of private key rather than only those held in one location.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by uninstalling a test Wallet Unit and confirming, by inspection of the device, that no associated private key material remains recoverable.

UNINST-11.3-02: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that all PID credentials and attestations stored in the Wallet Unit are irrecoverably deleted during uninstallation.

## Guidelines

- All PID credentials and attestations held in the Wallet Unit are irrecoverably deleted during uninstallation.
- Credential data left on the device after uninstallation could be recovered and would expose the Wallet User's identity attributes and attestation contents to whoever next obtained the device.
- Deletion removes the credential payloads from every on-device store in which they were held, so that no readable copy remains after uninstallation.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the documented deletion steps of the uninstallation procedure and the storage locations they cover for held credentials,

confirming that no credential data remains recoverable. Where a forensic examination is feasible, the CAB may also uninstall a test Wallet Unit holding credentials and inspect the device to confirm that no credential data remains recoverable.

UNINST-11.3-03: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that all cached data, temporary files, session tokens, and application state related to Wallet Unit operations are irrecoverably deleted during uninstallation.

## Guidelines

- All cached data, temporary files, session tokens, and application state relating to Wallet Unit operations are irrecoverably deleted during uninstallation.
- Residual caches, tokens, or state could reveal the Wallet User's activity or, in the case of session tokens, allow continued access to backend services after the Wallet Unit was supposedly gone.
- Deletion extends beyond the primary credential and key stores to the transient artefacts the Wallet Unit accumulates, so that operational residue is not left behind.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by uninstalling a test Wallet Unit and confirming that cached data, temporary files, session tokens, and application state have been removed.

UNINST-11.3-04: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that the WSCA and WSCD are cleared of all key material, configuration data, and application-specific data stored within them as part of the uninstallation process.

## Guidelines

- As part of uninstallation, the secure cryptographic application and secure cryptographic device are cleared of all key material, configuration data, and application-specific data held within them.
- If the secure hardware retained key material or configuration after uninstallation, a later installation or a forensic attacker could recover cryptographic secrets that were meant to be destroyed with the Wallet Unit.
- The uninstallation process invokes the operations that wipe the Wallet Unit's content from the secure cryptographic application and device, not only from ordinary application storage.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by uninstalling a test Wallet Unit and confirming that the secure cryptographic application and device no longer hold any Wallet-Unit key material, configuration, or data.

UNINST-11.3-05: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that, upon Wallet Instance uninstallation, all operational records and transaction logs associated with the uninstalled Wallet Unit that are held in the Wallet Provider's backend systems are either deleted or anonymised in accordance with the applicable data protection requirements, except where those records are required to be retained under a legal obligation, in which case the retained records shall be limited to what is strictly necessary, retained only for the minimum required period, and access-controlled to prevent use for any purpose other than compliance with that obligation.

## Guidelines

- The retention and disposal of operational records is governed by data protection regulations applicable to the Wallet Provider in its jurisdiction. Records that serve no purpose other than supporting wallet operation — such as transaction logs generated during normal wallet use — are not retained beyond the Wallet Unit's active lifetime unless a specific legal basis requires retention. Records subject to mandatory retention

are held only for the minimum required period and under access controls that limit their use to the specific compliance purpose.

- Without this control, the Wallet Provider could retain detailed transaction logs or operational records of a Wallet User's wallet use indefinitely after uninstallation, creating a risk that the data is used for purposes beyond the Wallet User's original consent — for example, profiling, secondary use, or disclosure to third parties. Indefinite retention of operational records after the termination of wallet operation is inconsistent with the data minimisation and storage limitation principles applicable to personal data.
- Anonymisation, where used in lieu of deletion, must reduce the data to a form from which the individual cannot be re-identified using reasonably available means. Pseudonymisation does not constitute anonymisation for this purpose. Wallet Providers with data retention obligations should document, for each retained record category: the legal basis, the retention period, the retention trigger, and the deletion trigger. The GDPR-compliant retention of audit logs after revocation is addressed separately in the revocation lifecycle event.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the Wallet Provider's documented data management policy and confirming that it includes procedures for handling transaction logs and operational records upon uninstallation, with enumerated record categories, documented legal bases, defined retention periods, and deletion mechanisms. The CAB may additionally verify the policy's implementation by reviewing records relating to previously uninstalled test Wallet Units and confirming deletion or anonymisation in accordance with the stated policy.

### 11.4 Revocation and Deregistration {#s-11-4}

UNINST-11.4-01: The Wallet Provider shall revoke the Wallet Instance Attestation and the Key Attestation associated with a Wallet Unit at the time of Wallet Instance uninstallation regardless of whether the Wallet User intends to install the Wallet Instance again on the same or a different device.

## Guidelines

- Revocation of the WUA upon uninstallation ensures that the Wallet Unit cannot be used for credential presentations after the Wallet Instance has been removed from the device. Uninstallation terminates the Wallet Unit's operational status. If the Wallet User wishes to use an EUDIW solution after uninstallation, they must install the Wallet Instance and complete the activation process to obtain a new Wallet Unit with a new WUA — the revoked Wallet Unit cannot be reused. Consistent with REV-12.2-08, this revocation applies to every Wallet Instance Attestation issued to the Wallet Unit, including those whose technical validity period has expired but whose revocation status the Wallet Provider still maintains.
- Without revocation upon uninstallation, the WUA remains valid for the remainder of its validity period after the Wallet Instance is removed from the device. A third party who recovers private key material from device storage before it is securely deleted, or from an unprotected backup, could use the valid WUA to make fraudulent credential presentations. The period between uninstallation and natural WUA expiry represents a window of potential fraudulent use that revocation eliminates.
- Revocation initiation occurs as part of the uninstallation flow, prior to the secure deletion of key material from the WSCD. Where the operating system performs uninstallation without Wallet User interaction or without invoking Wallet Provider processes (for example, automatic uninstallation by the device management system),

- the Wallet Provider establishes a mechanism for detecting such events and processing the associated revocation.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the Wallet Provider's documentation to confirm that the maximum revocation publication delay is defined and monitored, and by checking the Wallet Unit Attestation status list to confirm that a WUA revocation is published within the defined maximum delay. Where feasible, the CAB may also uninstall the Wallet Instance from a test device and attempt to make a presentation using key material from the uninstalled Wallet Unit, confirming that the WUA is rejected as revoked by the status check.

### 11.5 Verification of Complete Removal {#s-11-5}

UNINST-11.5-01: The Wallet Provider shall provide the Wallet User with confirmation that the uninstallation process has completed, including confirmation that the Wallet Unit has been deregistered with the Wallet Provider and has been revoked.

## Guidelines

- On completion, the Wallet Unit gives the Wallet User confirmation that uninstallation has finished, including that the Wallet Unit has been deregistered with the Wallet Provider and revoked.
- Without an explicit completion confirmation, a Wallet User could be unsure whether their credentials were actually removed and their Wallet Unit disabled, and might leave a partially removed Wallet Unit in place believing the opposite.
- The confirmation reports both the device-side completion and the backend outcome — deregistration and revocation — so that the Wallet User knows the Wallet Unit is fully retired.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by completing uninstallation and confirming that the Wallet User is shown confirmation covering deregistration and revocation.

UNINST-11.5-02: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that the uninstallation process results in no recoverable Wallet Unit data remaining on the device, including private keys, credentials, cached data, and application configuration files.

## Guidelines

- Uninstallation leaves no recoverable Wallet Unit data on the device, including private keys, credentials, cached data, and application configuration files.
- Any recoverable residue after uninstallation — keys, credentials, caches, or configuration — could be reconstructed by a later holder or forensic attacker into the Wallet User's identity data or usable credentials.
- This requirement is the end-state check over the deletion steps of this clause: after uninstallation, inspection of the device finds no recoverable Wallet Unit data of any listed category.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the documented deletion steps of the uninstallation procedure and the Wallet Unit data they cover, confirming that no recoverable Wallet Unit data remains. Where a forensic examination is feasible, the CAB may also inspect the device after uninstallation to confirm that no recoverable Wallet Unit data remains.

## 12 Lifecycle Event: Revocation (Permanent) {#s-12}

### 12.1 Revocation Triggers and Conditions {#s-12-1}

REV-12.1-01: The Wallet Provider shall implement mechanisms to detect security breaches affecting Wallet Units, including monitoring for indicators of device compromise, and shall initiate revocation procedures upon confirmed detection of a breach affecting a Wallet Unit.

## Guidelines

- The Wallet Provider has mechanisms to detect security breaches affecting Wallet Units, including watching for indicators of device compromise, and begins revocation once a breach affecting a Wallet Unit is confirmed.
- Without breach detection and a revocation trigger, a Wallet Unit known to be compromised could stay valid, allowing an attacker to continue presenting the Wallet User's credentials unchallenged.
- Detection draws on the indicators available to the Wallet Provider; on confirmation of a breach affecting a Wallet Unit, the revocation procedures of this chapter are initiated. The specific interactions monitored are described in clause 13.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the detection mechanisms and confirming that a confirmed breach affecting a test Wallet Unit triggers revocation.

REV-12.1-02: The Wallet Provider shall revoke a Wallet Unit when required to do so by applicable law or by a competent supervisory authority, within the timeframes mandated by the applicable legal requirement.

## Guidelines

- The Wallet Provider revokes a Wallet Unit when law or a competent supervisory authority requires it, within the timeframe the applicable legal requirement sets.
- If a legally mandated revocation were not carried out, or not within the required time, the Wallet Provider would be in breach of its obligations and a Wallet Unit that authorities have required to be stopped would remain usable.
- The Wallet Provider maintains a process to receive and act on legal and supervisory revocation requirements and to meet the mandated timeframes for each.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the process for handling legally mandated revocations and confirming that it provides for action within the applicable statutory timeframes.

REV-12.1-03: The Wallet Provider shall establish and maintain a documented procedure for accepting and processing requests for permanent revocation of a Wallet Unit submitted by an authorised party other than the Wallet Unit holder, including requests submitted in consequence of the death or legal incapacity of the natural person to whom the Wallet Unit is issued, and shall provide a mechanism that enables such requests to be submitted and verified without requiring participation of the Wallet Unit holder.

## Guidelines

- Permanent revocation may need to be initiated by parties other than the Wallet Unit holder — including legal representatives, next of kin acting under applicable law, or competent authorities — when the Wallet Unit holder dies or loses legal capacity. The revocation procedure accommodates these cases without requiring the Wallet Unit holder to authenticate, since by definition that is not possible.
- Without this control, a deceased person's Wallet Unit may remain in a valid state indefinitely, enabling third parties who gain access to the device — including malicious

- actors — to use the wallet for fraudulent transactions or identity claims. The absence of a revocation mechanism accessible to authorised third parties prevents timely deactivation of the Wallet Unit after the holder's death or incapacity.
- Verification of an authorised third party's right to request revocation may be achieved through a notarised document, a death certificate, a court order establishing legal incapacity, or another instrument recognised under applicable national law. The Wallet Provider's procedure specifies which instruments are acceptable and the identity verification steps applicable to the requestor. The procedure does not need to be automated — a manual review and processing path is acceptable provided the procedure is documented and consistently applied.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the Wallet Provider's documented procedure for third-party revocation requests and confirming that: (i) the procedure exists and covers the death and legal incapacity scenarios; (ii) it specifies acceptable verification instruments; (iii) it does not require participation by the Wallet Unit holder. The CAB may additionally submit a simulated third-party revocation request with appropriate documentation and verify that the request is processed and the Wallet Unit is revoked.

REV-12.1-04: The Wallet Provider shall establish processes for Wallet Users or other competent parties to notify suspected device compromise.

## Guidelines

- The Wallet Provider provides ways for Wallet Users and other competent parties to report a suspected device compromise.
- If there were no route to report a suspected compromise, the Wallet User who first notices something wrong would have no way to raise the alarm, and the Wallet Provider would learn of the problem only once damage had been done.
- The reporting routes are reachable by the Wallet User and by other competent parties, and feed into the Wallet Provider's detection and revocation.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by confirming that documented reporting routes exist for Wallet Users and other competent parties and that a submitted report reaches the Wallet Provider's revocation process.

REV-12.1-05: The Wallet Provider shall revoke a Wallet Unit for which credible evidence of fraudulent use or sufficient indication of suspected compromise has been identified and shall record the basis and supporting evidence for the revocation decision.

## Guidelines

- The Wallet Provider revokes a Wallet Unit for which there is credible evidence of fraudulent use or sufficient indication of suspected compromise, and records the basis and supporting evidence for that decision.
- Without acting on credible evidence of fraud or compromise, the Wallet Provider would leave an attacker-controlled Wallet Unit in service; without recording the basis, a revocation could not be justified afterwards or distinguished from an unfounded one.
- The decision rests on credible evidence or sufficient indication, and the Wallet Provider keeps a record of that basis and the supporting evidence so the decision is accountable and reviewable.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing revocation records and confirming that revocations on grounds of fraud or suspected compromise are supported by a recorded basis and evidence.

REV-12.1-06: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that a Wallet User can initiate revocation of their own Wallet Unit through a means that does not depend on access to the Wallet Unit’s device, on authentication factors or credentials that are typically kept or carried together with that device, or on any secret or credential that the Wallet User would typically only store in a fixed location such as their home.

## Guidelines

- There is at least one route by which the Wallet User can trigger revocation of their own Wallet Unit that does not need the device itself, does not rely on something normally lost with it — a revocation code stored on or beside the device, or an identity document carried in the same bag as the phone — and does not rely on anything the Wallet User could reach only by first returning to a fixed place such as home. The route works from wherever the Wallet User happens to be when they need it.
- The scenario this addresses is a device stolen away from home, often together with the Wallet User’s identity documents — a bag taken abroad. If the only way to revoke needs the phone, needs a passport or code that was taken with it, or needs a code the Wallet User keeps safely at home, the Wallet User cannot stop the wallet from being abused while travelling, and being unable to revoke leaves it open to attack for far longer than any denial-of-service would cost.
- Acceptable approaches include a revocation route knowledge the Wallet User carries in memory (for instance answers on questions that only the user should be able to give), or re-verification by the Wallet Provider through channels that need no pre-stored token.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the Wallet User-initiated revocation design and confirming that at least one route does not depend on the device, on credentials typically lost with it, or on a secret the Wallet User would keep only at a fixed location such as home, for instance by inspecting the design and, where feasible, by initiating revocation from a different device, and from a different location, without the original authentication means.

REV-12.1-07: The Wallet Provider shall, after authenticating the PID Provider as the sender, revoke a Wallet Unit when the PID Provider forwards a request for revocation of that Wallet Unit on behalf of the person in whose name a PID was issued to it.

## Guidelines

- The Wallet Provider acts on a revocation request that the PID Provider forwards for the person.
- A person recognises a stolen Wallet Unit from an overview at the PID Provider, and a Wallet Provider that ignores the forwarded request leaves the Wallet Unit active.
- The request is received through an authenticated interface between the PID Provider and the Wallet Provider. The revocation then follows clause 11.2, including REV-12.202.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the interface and its authentication and by examining records of requests received and the revocations that followed.

REV-12.1-08: The Wallet Provider shall treat a notice from the PID Provider of the decease of a Wallet Holder as a request under REV-12.1-03 for permanent revocation of the Wallet Unit to which the notice relates.

## Guidelines

- A decease notice from the PID Provider has the same effect as a request submitted by an authorised third party.

- Without it, a deceased person's Wallet Unit stays active until someone else asks for revocation, and can be used for fraud.
- The Wallet Provider authenticates the sender as in REV-12.1-07 and does not require participation of the holder.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the procedure and by examining records of past notices.

### 12.2 Revocation Procedures {#s-12-2}

REV-12.2-01: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that revocation requests submitted by parties other than the Wallet User are subject to verification of the authority of the requesting party to trigger revocation before the request is acted upon.

## Guidelines

- A revocation request from anyone other than the Wallet User is acted on only after the Wallet Provider has verified that the requesting party has the authority to trigger revocation.
- The control guards against a denial-of-service in which a party with no standing has a Wallet User's Wallet Unit revoked, or the service is disrupted by spurious requests. It is balanced against timeliness: where verifying authority - or, for the Wallet User's own request, authenticating - imposes a threshold a legitimate requester cannot meet in time, the harm of a Wallet Unit that stays active and open to attack can far outweigh the harm of an unwarranted revocation. The accessibility of the Wallet User's own revocation path under adverse conditions is the subject of a separate requirement in clause 12.1.
- The Wallet Provider establishes the requesting party's authority — legal standing or a defined role — before acting on a third-party revocation request, distinguishing it from a request by the Wallet User themselves.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by submitting third-party revocation requests with and without demonstrated authority and confirming that only the authorised request is acted upon.

REV-12.2-02: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that a revoked Wallet Unit is disabled within a defined maximum timeframe following the revocation decision.

## Guidelines

- A revoked Wallet Unit is disabled within a defined maximum time after the revocation decision.
- If disabling could be delayed indefinitely, a Wallet Unit already decided to be revoked — perhaps because it is compromised — would stay usable in the gap, and the revocation would not achieve its purpose in time.
- The Wallet Provider bounds the interval between the revocation decision and the effective disabling of the Wallet Unit by a defined maximum, and operates so that disabling occurs within it.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the documented revocation mechanism and confirming that a triggered revocation disables the Wallet Unit within the defined maximum timeframe, corroborating this against revocation records. Where feasible, the CAB may also trigger a revocation and confirm that the Wallet Unit is disabled within the defined maximum timeframe.

REV-12.2-03: The Wallet Provider shall document and enforce that maximum permissible delay between the revocation decision and the effective disabling of the Wallet Unit.

## Guidelines

- The Wallet Provider documents the maximum permissible delay between a revocation decision and the effective disabling of the Wallet Unit, and enforces it.
- An undocumented or unenforced delay would leave the timeliness of revocation undefined, so that neither the Wallet User nor an auditor could tell how long a revoked Wallet Unit might remain usable.
- The maximum delay is written down as a defined value and the Wallet Provider's operations are arranged to keep within it, making the disabling timeframe of the preceding requirement concrete and auditable.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the documented maximum delay and confirming, against revocation records, that the effective disabling times observed fall within it.

REV-12.2-04: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that, upon revocation of a Wallet Unit, the revocation status of the associated Wallet Instance Attestation and Key Attestation is published to the applicable revocation status mechanism without undue delay, enabling parties interacting with the Wallet Unit to detect the revocation prior to accepting transactions with the revoked Wallet Unit.

## Guidelines

- This requirement addresses the window between the moment a Wallet Unit is revoked and the moment that revocation becomes observable to parties querying the WUA revocation status. During this window a party checking the status mechanism would not detect the revocation and would treat the Wallet Unit as valid. The requirement obliges the Wallet Provider to minimise this window by publishing the updated revocation status to the applicable mechanism as promptly as possible after the revocation decision is confirmed.
- Publication of the WUA revocation status is achieved through the status mechanism defined in the relevant ecosystem trust infrastructure.
- Relying parties that cache revocation status responses and check them at a lower frequency than the WUA revocation publishing interval may not detect revocation immediately. This is acceptable provided the Wallet Provider’s documented publishing latency falls within the agreed ecosystem parameters.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the Wallet Provider's documented maximum publishing delay and corroborating, against revocation records, that revocation status becomes observable through the applicable status mechanism within that delay. Where feasible, the CAB may also revoke a Wallet Unit and measure the time until the revocation status is observable, confirming it falls within the documented maximum publishing delay.

REV-12.2-05: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that the Wallet Instance ceases to display the European Digital Identity Wallet Trust Mark referred to in [13] from the moment the Wallet Instance Attestation of that Wallet Unit is revoked.

## Guidelines

- The Trust Mark signals to the Wallet User, and to anyone the Wallet User shows the application to, that the wallet in use is a recognised European Digital Identity Wallet. Once the Wallet Unit is revoked that statement is no longer true and the mark is withdrawn.

- A revoked Wallet Unit that keeps displaying the mark misleads the Wallet User into continuing to rely on it, and can be used by an attacker in possession of the device to convince a third party in a face-to-face situation that a revoked wallet is still recognised.
- A conformant implementation ties the display of the mark to the current revocation state of the Wallet Instance Attestation rather than to a value cached at installation, so that the mark disappears at the next launch after revocation even when the Wallet Unit is offline at the moment of revocation.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the documented Trust Mark behaviour and confirming that the Trust Mark is no longer displayed once a Wallet Unit is revoked. Where feasible, the CAB may also revoke a test Wallet Unit and confirm, on the device, that the Trust Mark is no longer displayed.

REV-12.2-06: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that revocation of a Wallet Unit is permanent and irreversible, and shall not provide any mechanism, interface, process, or administrative function through which a permanently revoked Wallet Unit can be restored to an active or operational state.

## Guidelines

- Permanent revocation terminates the Wallet Unit's validity definitively. The Wallet Unit cannot be re-activated, re-registered, or otherwise returned to an operational state following permanent revocation. If the same natural person wishes to use an EUDIW solution after their Wallet Unit has been permanently revoked, they undergo the full installation and activation process to obtain a new Wallet Unit, which constitutes a new Wallet Unit rather than a restoration of the previously revoked one.
- Without this control, an administrative override or software interface that restores a revoked Wallet Unit would undermine the integrity of the revocation mechanism. An attacker who gains access to the Wallet Provider's backend systems — or an insider with administrative access — could reverse a revocation performed in response to a security compromise, re-enabling a Wallet Unit whose associated private key material or credentials may have been exposed to an adversary.
