- Systems and procedures that would otherwise allow administrative restoration of revoked Wallet Units — such as database entries, administrative panels, or API endpoints capable of toggling revocation status — should be identified and their absence confirmed through audit. Where a Wallet Provider offers a re-issuance service enabling a Wallet User to obtain a new Wallet Unit after revocation, this is distinct from re-activation: re-issuance produces a new Wallet Unit with new WUA and new key material, not a restoration of the previously revoked Wallet Unit.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the Wallet Provider's system documentation and confirming the absence of any functionality that permits reversal of permanent revocation. The CAB also attempts to re-activate a test Wallet Unit that has been permanently revoked and confirms that no pathway — including administrative or technical — allows this. The CAB additionally reviews the Wallet Provider's access control documentation to confirm that no personnel role has the capability to reverse a permanent revocation.

REV-12.2-07: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that the Wallet Instance Attestation issued to each Wallet Unit contains a reference to the revocation status mechanism maintained by the Wallet Provider, enabling relying parties and PID Providers to determine the current revocation status of the Wallet Unit at the time of any transaction.

## Guidelines

- The Wallet Unit Attestation (WUA) serves as the primary artefact by which relying parties and PID Providers verify the legitimacy and current status of a Wallet Unit. Including a reference to the revocation status mechanism in the WUA enables these parties to check the current revocation status at the point of transaction, rather than relying solely on the expiry date of the WUA. This is particularly relevant in the period between revocation and WUA expiry, during which the WUA remains technically valid but the Wallet Unit must not be accepted.
- Without this control, a relying party or PID Provider that receives a presentation from a revoked Wallet Unit cannot determine from the WUA alone where to check whether that Wallet Unit has been permanently revoked. This increases the risk that transactions are accepted from permanently revoked Wallet Units, undermining the intended effect of revocation and potentially enabling continued fraudulent use of a Wallet Unit whose private key material has been compromised.
- The revocation status mechanism reference is typically a URL pointing to a revocation status list, an OCSP endpoint, or an equivalent status service. The format and content of this reference are determined by the applicable ecosystem trust framework and credential format specification. The Wallet Provider maintains this endpoint and ensures it is accessible to relying parties and PID Providers without requiring authentication.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by inspecting the WUA of a test Wallet Unit and confirming the presence of a revocation status mechanism reference. The CAB then uses that reference to query the revocation status of the Wallet Unit and confirms that the response correctly reflects the Wallet Unit's current status, including after the test Wallet Unit has been permanently revoked. The CAB also confirms that the revocation status endpoint is publicly accessible without requiring authentication.

REV-12.2-08: The Wallet Provider shall, whenever it revokes the Wallet Instance Attestation of a Wallet Unit — on revocation of the Wallet Unit under this clause, on uninstallation of the Wallet Instance, or on revocation of a source Wallet Unit during migration — set to revoked the revocation status of every Wallet Instance Attestation it has issued to that Wallet Unit, including any such attestation whose technical validity period has expired but whose revocation status the Wallet Provider still maintains, so that the revocation status reference recorded by a PID Provider or Attestation Provider at issuance reflects the revocation throughout the lifetime of the PID or attestation issued against it.

## Guidelines

- A Wallet Unit is issued many Wallet Instance Attestations over its lifetime through successive re-issuance under ACT-6.2-10, each carrying its own revocation status reference under ACT-6.2-05. A PID Provider or Attestation Provider detects revocation of the Wallet Unit through the revocation status reference of the specific Wallet Instance Attestation it validated at issuance. A Wallet Instance Attestation has a technical validity period of less than 24 hours under ACT-6.2-09, while the PID or attestation it supports remains valid for far longer, so for most of that lifetime the recorded reference identifies a Wallet Instance Attestation that has passed its technical validity. Setting the revoked status on every Wallet Instance Attestation issued to the

Wallet Unit, including expired ones whose revocation status remains maintained, keeps the recorded reference meaningful for the whole life of the PID or attestation.

- Without this control, revocation of a Wallet Unit sets the revoked status only on the currently valid Wallet Instance Attestation. A PID Provider that checks the reference it recorded at issuance, which by then identifies an expired Wallet Instance Attestation, does not observe the revocation and continues to treat the Wallet Unit as valid. An attacker who retains a revoked Wallet Unit thereby keeps its already-issued PID acceptable until that PID separately expires or is revoked, defeating the purpose of the revocation.
- Acceptable approaches include recording, for each Wallet Unit, the status list entries of all Wallet Instance Attestations issued to it and setting every such entry to revoked in a single revocation action; and retaining those entries on the status list for as long as any PID or attestation issued against the Wallet Unit remains in use, independently of the technical validity period of the individual Wallet Instance Attestation.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the Wallet Provider's documented revocation procedure and confirming that a single revocation action sets to revoked the status of every Wallet Instance Attestation issued to the Wallet Unit, including those past their technical validity period whose status is still maintained, and by inspecting revocation records for a revoked Wallet Unit to confirm that the status list entries of its earlier, expired Wallet Instance Attestations were also set. Where feasible, the CAB may issue to a test Wallet Unit more than one Wallet Instance Attestation, allow the earlier attestation to expire, revoke the Wallet Unit, and confirm that both the expired and the current entries reflect revocation within the maximum publication delay documented under REV-12.3-01.

### 12.3 Impact on PIDs and Attestations {#s-12-3}

REV-12.3-01: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that the revocation status of the Wallet Instance Attestation and of the Key Attestation is published to the applicable attestation status list within a defined and documented maximum time period following the triggering event for revocation, and shall make that attestation status list available in a format and at a location that enables PID Providers and Attestation Providers to query the revocation status of any such attestation without requiring authenticated access to the status service.

## Guidelines

- PID Providers and Attestation Providers that have issued credentials to a Wallet Unit need to be able to determine whether that Wallet Unit's attestation has been revoked, in order to decide whether to revoke or suspend the credentials they issued. The primary mechanism for this determination is the Wallet Unit Attestation status list, which the Wallet Provider maintains and updates. Timely publication of the revocation status to this list enables the pull-based discovery model that allows PID Providers and Attestation Providers to act on the revocation without direct notification.
- A delayed update to the Wallet Unit Attestation status list creates a window during which PID Providers and Attestation Providers, querying the status list, incorrectly conclude that a revoked Wallet Unit's attestation is still valid. During this window, PID Providers may continue to issue or accept renewal requests from the revoked Wallet Unit, and relying parties may continue to accept credential presentations from it. The length of this window is directly determined by the Wallet Provider's publication delay.
- The maximum time period for revocation status publication is defined based on the operational requirements and risk profile of the Wallet Provider. Where revocation is triggered by a security compromise, the publication delay is minimised. The Wallet

- Provider documents the maximum publication delay for each trigger type and monitors compliance. The status list is accessible publicly — without authentication — to enable any PID Provider or Attestation Provider to query it.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the Wallet Provider's documented maximum revocation publication delay for each trigger type and confirming, against revocation records, that the updated revocation status is published on the status list within that delay and that the status list is accessible without authentication. Where feasible, the CAB may also trigger a test revocation, measure the time between the trigger event and publication of the updated status, and attempt to access the status list without authentication, confirming that the query succeeds and returns the correct status for the revoked Wallet Unit Attestation.

REV-12.3-02: [CONDITIONAL] Where the Wallet Instance Attestation or the Key Attestation is issued in the mobile document format specified in [11], the Wallet Provider shall publish its revocation status by means of an attestation status list or an attestation revocation list as specified in [12].

## Guidelines

- The mechanism through which revocation status is published depends on the format in which the attestation was issued, because each format defines its own status representation. For the mobile document format both a status list and a revocation list are available.
- Where a Wallet Provider publishes status in a representation the receiving party cannot parse for the format at hand, that party cannot determine the revocation state and either accepts a revoked attestation or rejects a valid one, in both cases without detecting that the check itself failed.
- A conformant implementation selects the publication mechanism from the attestation format at issuance time and records that choice in the attestation itself, so that a receiving party knows where and how to look.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by determining the format of the attestations issued in production, retrieving the published status information, and confirming that its representation is the one specified for that format.

REV-12.3-03: [CONDITIONAL] Where the Wallet Instance Attestation or the Key Attestation is issued in the selectively disclosable JSON Web Token verifiable credential format, the Wallet Provider shall publish its revocation status by means of an attestation status list as specified in [10].

## Guidelines

- For the selectively disclosable JSON Web Token format a status list is the only defined representation; a revocation list is not an available alternative.
- Where a revocation list is published for this format, a receiving party following the specification looks for a status list, does not find one, and is not able to proceed by lack of usable revocation check, so a possibly valid attestation is refused, leading to an unusable Wallet Unit.
- A conformant implementation publishes a status list and records its location and the index of the attestation within it in the attestation itself.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by retrieving the status information referenced by an attestation issued in this format and confirming that it is a status list in the specified representation.

### 12.4 Data Deletion Requirements {#s-12-4}

REV-12.4-01: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that all private keys stored in the remote WSCD that are associated with a revoked Wallet Unit are irrecoverably deleted and that the revocation event is recorded in a tamper-evident audit log.

## Guidelines

- All private keys in the remote secure cryptographic device that belong to a revoked Wallet Unit are irrecoverably deleted, and the revocation event is written to a tamperevident audit log.
- If a revoked Wallet Unit's server-held private keys were left in place, they could still be used to produce valid signatures for the Wallet User; without a tamper-evident log, a revocation could be quietly reversed or denied.
- On revocation, the Wallet Provider destroys the associated keys in the remote secure cryptographic device and records the event in a log whose entries cannot be altered undetectably.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the documented server-side key handling and confirming that revocation of a Wallet Unit whose keys are held server-side deletes those keys and that a tamper-evident log entry records the revocation. Where feasible, the CAB may also revoke a test Wallet Unit whose keys are held server-side and confirm that those keys are deleted and that a tamper-evident log entry records the revocation.

REV-12.4-02: The Wallet Provider shall ensure that, following permanent revocation of a Wallet Unit, all personal data associated with the revoked Wallet Unit that is held in the Wallet Provider's backend systems is deleted or anonymised in accordance with the applicable data protection requirements, except where those records are required to be retained under a legal obligation, in which case the retained data shall be limited to what is strictly necessary, retained only for the minimum required period, and access-controlled to prevent use for any purpose other than compliance with that obligation.

## Guidelines

- Personal data held by the Wallet Provider following revocation may include identityrelated records generated during PID issuance, transaction logs, correspondence relating to the Wallet Unit's operation, and records of the revocation event itself. Following revocation, the legal basis for retaining personal data — typically the contractual relationship between the Wallet User and the Wallet Provider — terminates, triggering data subject rights including the right to erasure, except where a separate legal basis mandates retention.
- Without this control, the Wallet Provider may retain personal data associated with a permanently revoked Wallet Unit beyond the period for which there is a legal basis to do so. This exposes the data to risks of secondary use, unauthorised access, or data breaches affecting individuals who have terminated their relationship with the Wallet Provider — whether by choice or as a consequence of a security incident that triggered the revocation.
- Retention obligations that may apply after revocation include, but are not limited to, audit logs required by national e-government regulations, tax or financial records, and records required by anti-money laundering legislation. For each category of retained data, the Wallet Provider documents the specific legal basis, the retention period, and the deletion or anonymisation trigger. Anonymisation used as an alternative to deletion must meet a standard at which re-identification is not reasonably achievable using available means.

- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the Wallet Provider's documented data retention policy for the post-revocation period and confirming that: (i) categories of retained data are enumerated with a documented legal basis and defined retention period for each; (ii) deletion or anonymisation is triggered at the end of the retention period; (iii) access to retained data is restricted to the specific compliance purpose. The CAB may additionally review records relating to previously revoked test Wallet Units to confirm that retention and deletion are applied in accordance with the documented policy.

REV-12.4-03: The Wallet Provider shall retain audit logs related to Wallet Unit revocation for a period sufficient to support legal proceedings, supervisory audit, and incident investigation, and shall ensure that the retention period does not exceed the maximum period permitted under applicable data protection law.

## Guidelines

- The Wallet Provider keeps revocation audit logs long enough to support legal proceedings, supervisory audit, and incident investigation, but no longer than the maximum period the applicable data protection law allows.
- Logs discarded too soon would leave the Wallet Provider unable to demonstrate that a revocation was justified or to support an investigation; logs kept too long would breach data protection limits and create needless exposure of personal data.
- The retention period is set to meet the legal, supervisory, and investigative need while staying within the maximum permitted by the applicable data protection framework, and is applied consistently to revocation logs.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the retention policy for revocation logs and confirming that the period is sufficient for the stated purposes and does not exceed the maximum permitted by applicable data protection law.

## 13 Monitoring and Fraud Management {#s-13}

NOTE: The requirements in the present clause apply to a Wallet Unit throughout its active lifetime and in every lifecycle state, except where an individual requirement is explicitly conditioned on a particular state. They address the detection of, and response to, compromise and fraudulent use of a Wallet Unit and its ecosystem. Monitoring of whether the solution remains sufficiently secure and compliant as its technical and regulatory environment evolves is a distinct activity, addressed in clause 9.7.

### 13.1 General Monitoring and Fraud Detection {#s-13-1}

MON-13.1-01: The Wallet Provider shall operate a monitoring capability that detects, across every lifecycle state of a Wallet Unit, patterns indicative of compromise or fraudulent use in the backend interactions it receives from that Wallet Unit, including a frequency of those interactions inconsistent with normal operation and a device or Wallet Secure Cryptographic Device profile presented in an interaction that is inconsistent with the profile recorded for that Wallet Unit at activation or at a subsequent re-attestation.

## Guidelines

- The monitoring capability draws only on interactions the Wallet Provider actually receives, because it operates the corresponding backend service — for example attestation status queries, software update check-ins, trust anchor distribution, migration-initiation requests, and reports of suspected compromise. Relying party interactions and credential presentations do not pass through the Wallet Provider, so how a Wallet Unit is used towards relying parties is deliberately not observable to it and is not a monitoring input. The interactions available differ by lifecycle state and are set out in clause 13.2.
- A Wallet Unit taken over by an attacker frequently leaves no trace in any usage record, because presentations are not visible to the Wallet Provider. The takeover surfaces instead in the pattern of the Wallet Unit’s own contacts with the Wallet Provider — an unexplained burst of status queries, repeated failed update check-ins, or a device or Wallet Secure Cryptographic Device profile in a later interaction that no longer matches the one established at activation.
- Acceptable approaches include frequency thresholds on the interactions the Wallet Provider receives, and comparison of the device and Wallet Secure Cryptographic Device profile presented at each interaction against the profile recorded during Wallet Unit activation, established under clauses 6.1 and 6.2. The specific interactions monitored in each lifecycle state are those set out in clause 13.2.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the monitoring design and the backend interactions it consumes, and by reproducing each listed condition — an abnormal interaction frequency and a mismatched device profile — against a test Wallet Unit and confirming that the monitoring capability records it.

MON-13.1-02: The Wallet Provider shall document, for each anomaly condition detected under MON-13.1-01, the investigation procedure applied and the response available, up to and including revocation of the Wallet Unit.

## Guidelines

- Detection has value only where a defined response follows it. The documentation ties each condition to who acts on it, within what time, and with what powers.

- Where responses are left to the judgement of whoever is on duty, comparable incidents are handled inconsistently, the decision to revoke is deferred out of caution, and an attacker retains a usable Wallet Unit for longer than necessary.
- The documented responses are normally graded, from recording the observation, through notifying the Wallet User, to revocation of the Wallet Unit. The conditions under which a Wallet Unit is revoked are set out in clause 12.1.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the documented conditions and responses, and by sampling recorded anomalies to confirm that the response actually applied was the documented one.

MON-13.1-03: The Wallet Provider shall provide the Wallet User with a means of reporting suspected compromise or misuse of a Wallet Unit that does not require the Wallet User to authenticate to that Wallet Unit.

## Guidelines

- The Wallet User is frequently the first to notice that something is wrong. The reporting channel is reachable even when the Wallet Unit itself cannot be used, which is precisely the situation in a takeover.
- Where the only reporting route runs through the Wallet Unit, a Wallet User locked out by an attacker who has changed the authentication factors has no way to raise the alarm, and the Wallet Provider receives no signal at all.
- This is the same reporting channel as the one required by MAINT-9.5-03 for reporting loss or theft of the device, so that the Wallet User has one route to remember rather than several, regardless of the lifecycle state the Wallet Unit is in at the time.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by locating the reporting channel as a Wallet User would, submitting a test report without authenticating to the Wallet Unit, and confirming that the report reaches the monitoring or support function.

### 13.2 State-Specific Monitoring Inputs {#s-13-2}

MON-13.2-01: [CONDITIONAL] For a Wallet Unit that holds no PID credential, the Wallet Provider shall base the monitoring required under MON-13.1-01 on the Wallet Instance Attestation and Key Attestation status queries, the software update check-ins, and the reports of suspected compromise that it receives from the Wallet Unit at that stage.

## Guidelines

- In no lifecycle state does the Wallet Provider observe how a Wallet Unit is used towards relying parties: credential presentations pass directly between the Wallet Unit and the relying party, and the Wallet Provider is deliberately kept outside that path, so monitoring never draws on usage data. Before a PID has been issued, the interactions the Wallet Provider does receive — because it operates the corresponding backend service — are the Wallet Instance Attestation and Key Attestation status queries, the software update check-ins, and any report of suspected compromise the Wallet Instance itself generates. This requirement fixes the monitoring inputs for the state before PID issuance to those interactions.
- An attacker who takes over a Wallet Unit before PID issuance leaves no trace in any usage log, because none exists yet. The only place the takeover can surface is in the pattern of the Wallet Unit’s own contacts with the Wallet Provider — an unexplained burst of status queries, repeated failed update check-ins, or a device profile in a later interaction that no longer matches the one established at activation.

- Acceptable approaches include frequency thresholds on status queries and update check-ins, and comparison of the device and Wallet Secure Cryptographic Device profile presented at each interaction against the profile recorded during Wallet Unit activation, established under clauses 6.1 and 6.2.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reproducing each listed condition — an abnormal query frequency and a mismatched device profile — against a test Wallet Unit that holds no PID credential and confirming that the monitoring capability records it.

MON-13.2-02: [CONDITIONAL] For a Wallet Unit that holds a PID credential, the Wallet Provider shall extend the monitoring required under MON-13.1-01 to the trust anchor distribution channel, the software update check-ins, and any migration-initiation request it receives from the Wallet Unit.

## Guidelines

- Once a PID credential is present, the Wallet Provider gains backend touchpoints beyond those available before PID issuance: the authenticated channel used to distribute trust anchors, the ongoing software update check-ins, and any request to initiate migration to a new device. This requirement adds those interactions to the monitoring inputs for a Wallet Unit in this state.
- A takeover occurring after PID issuance — for example through a compromised device later used to initiate a fraudulent migration — would otherwise go undetected until it results in a Wallet User complaint or a downstream relying party dispute.
- Acceptable approaches apply the same frequency and device-profile checks used before PID issuance to the trust anchor distribution channel, to update check-ins, and to migration-initiation requests, comparing the pattern of these interactions against the profile established for the Wallet Unit at activation and at each subsequent reattestation.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reproducing an anomalous condition — an abnormal trust anchor distribution or migration-initiation pattern — on a test Wallet Unit that holds a PID credential and confirming that the monitoring capability records it.

### 13.3 Monitoring of the Application and Web Ecosystem {#s-13-3}

MON-13.3-01: The Wallet Provider shall monitor the application distribution channels through which the Wallet Instance is made available for counterfeit, modified, or look-alike applications that impersonate the Wallet Instance.

## Guidelines

- Monitoring covers the application stores and other distribution channels on which a Wallet User could plausibly search for and obtain the Wallet Instance. A look-alike application is one that reproduces the name, icon, branding, or description of the genuine Wallet Instance closely enough that a Wallet User could install it in mistake for the genuine one.
- An attacker who publishes a counterfeit Wallet Instance can capture the credentials, authentication factors, and personal data of every Wallet User who installs it in mistake for the genuine application, without ever compromising the Wallet Provider’s own systems. The Wallet Provider is the party best placed to recognise an impersonation of its own application at scale.
- Acceptable approaches include periodic automated searches of the major application stores for the Wallet Instance’s name, publisher, and iconography, third-party brandprotection monitoring services, and a channel through which Wallet Users can report a suspected counterfeit application.

- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the documented monitoring process and its coverage of the distribution channels through which the Wallet Instance is offered, and by reviewing records of counterfeit applications identified over a representative period.

MON-13.3-02: The Wallet Provider shall, upon identifying a counterfeit, modified, or lookalike application that impersonates the Wallet Instance, pursue its removal from the application distribution channel on which it is offered.

## Guidelines

- Pursuing removal means initiating and following through the takedown or abusereporting procedure of the distribution channel concerned, and escalating where the initial report does not result in removal. The obligation is one of diligent action, since the decision to remove ultimately rests with the operator of the distribution channel.
- A counterfeit application that is detected but left in place continues to harvest the data of Wallet Users who install it. Detection without a removal obligation would leave the Wallet Provider aware of an active impersonation of its application and taking no action to end it.
- Acceptable approaches include using the application store’s established trademark and impersonation reporting mechanisms, retaining evidence of each report and its outcome, and escalating unresolved cases. Identification of the counterfeit application is addressed by MON-13.3-01.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing records of counterfeit applications identified under MON-13.3-01 and confirming that a removal request was raised for each and pursued to a recorded outcome.

MON-13.3-03: The Wallet Provider shall monitor for websites that impersonate the Wallet Provider in order to deceive Wallet Users.

## Guidelines

- Monitoring covers websites that reproduce the Wallet Provider’s name, branding, or domain closely enough to be mistaken for an official site — for example a site offering a supposed download of the Wallet Instance, or a site soliciting the Wallet User’s credentials or personal data under the guise of the Wallet Provider.
- A convincing impersonation website can be used to distribute a counterfeit Wallet Instance, to phish authentication factors or recovery material, or to induce the Wallet User to disclose personal data. As with a counterfeit application, the Wallet Provider is the party best placed to recognise an impersonation of its own identity.
- Acceptable approaches include domain-monitoring and brand-protection services that detect newly registered look-alike domains, monitoring of certificate transparency logs for certificates issued against look-alike domains, and a Wallet User reporting channel. Takedown of an identified website is addressed by MON-13.3-04.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the documented monitoring process and reviewing records of impersonation websites identified over a representative period.

MON-13.3-04: The Wallet Provider shall, upon identifying a website that impersonates the Wallet Provider or the Wallet Instance, pursue its takedown.

## Guidelines

- Pursuing takedown means initiating and following through the applicable abusereporting, registrar, or hosting-provider procedure to have the impersonation website removed, and escalating where an initial request does not result in removal. As with a counterfeit application, the obligation is one of diligent action, the final decision resting with the registrar or hosting provider.

- An impersonation website that is detected but left in place continues to deceive Wallet Users, distribute counterfeit software, or harvest credentials. Detection without a takedown obligation would leave the Wallet Provider aware of an active impersonation of its identity and taking no action to end it.
- Acceptable approaches include reporting to the domain registrar, the hosting provider, and the relevant abuse and anti-phishing services, retaining evidence of each request and its outcome, and escalating unresolved cases. Identification of the website is addressed by MON-13.3-03.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing records of impersonation websites identified under MON-13.3-03 and confirming that a takedown request was raised for each and pursued to a recorded outcome.

### 13.4 Wallet User Warning Channel {#s-13-4}

MON-13.4-01: The Wallet Provider shall maintain a means of contacting the Wallet User over a push channel that the Wallet User will see without opening the Wallet Instance and that is independent of the Wallet Instance, for use in warning the Wallet User when compromise of the Wallet Unit is suspected.

## Guidelines

- A channel independent of the Wallet Instance is one that does not rely on the Wallet Instance being installed, functional, or under the Wallet User’s control in order to reach the Wallet User — for example SMS, telephone call or message through a separate messaging service. The channel is a push channel: the Wallet Provider actively delivers the warning to the Wallet User rather than leaving it to be discovered. A pull channel — such as a message placed in a portal or inbox that the Wallet User has to decide to open — is not sufficient, because the Wallet User might open it only days later, by which time a warning about a suspected compromise would arrive too late to act on. The Wallet User therefore sees the warning promptly and by ordinary means, rather than only on next opening an application or web portal that could be compromised or inaccessible.
- An attacker who has taken over the Wallet Unit, or the device on which it runs, controls what the Wallet User sees inside the Wallet Instance and can suppress an inapplication warning. A warning delivered only through the Wallet Instance therefore cannot be relied upon in exactly the circumstances — a suspected compromise — for which it is most needed.
- Acceptable approaches include a phone number or messaging contact obtained from the Wallet User, with consent, at or after activation, or an operating-system notification mechanism that does not depend on the Wallet Instance session. Where the Wallet Provider deliberately holds no data identifying the Wallet User, the channel is designed consistently with that data-minimisation objective — for example an alternate contact agreed in advance and stored separately from any identity data — and the design of the channel is documented.
- A CAB verifies this requirement by reviewing the documented contact channel and confirming it is independent of the Wallet Instance and that it actively pushes a warning rather than waiting to be read, so that a suspected compromise warning reaches the Wallet User without the Wallet Instance being opened and without the Wallet User having to open a portal or inbox to find it. Where feasible, the CAB may also trigger a test suspected-compromise warning and confirm that it reaches the Wallet User in this way.

## Annex A (informative): Lifecycle State Diagram {#s-a}

NOTE: This annex is informative and does not contain normative requirements.

This annex illustrates the lifecycle states of a Wallet Unit and the transitions between them. It is informative; the normative requirements are those in clauses 3.5 to 13. Figure A.1 shows the states and the lifecycle events that move a Wallet Unit between them, and the paragraphs that follow describe each state.

Figure A.1 — Wallet Unit lifecycle states and transitions

![Image](/img/edi-stelsel/2026-11-06/nl-p-04w/image_000000_e5bbd568625eb70a4e5998df9aa67d54b4148e42538ba621a3f3ffec85448d7c.png)

Installed. The Wallet Instance has been installed on the device but the Wallet Unit has not yet been activated; no keys, attestations or credentials are present. This state is governed by clause 3.5. It is entered when installation completes and left when the Wallet User activates the Wallet Unit.

Operational without PID. The Wallet Unit has been activated — the secure cryptographic device and application are initialised and the Wallet Unit holds its Wallet Instance Attestation and Key Attestation — but no PID credential is present. In this state the Wallet Unit can hold and present non-identity attestations, subject to clause 7. Activation is governed by clause 6. In implementations where the Wallet Unit Attestation is issued only at the start of PID issuance, a Wallet Unit passes through this state only briefly before PID issuance begins.

Valid. A PID credential is present and active and the Wallet Unit is fully operational for identification and for the presentation of PID-dependent attestations. The transition into this state is PID issuance, governed by clause 8. While in this state the Wallet Unit is maintained — software updates, key rotation, attestation renewal and credential lifecycle management — under clause 9, and is monitored under clause 13; these activities return the Wallet Unit to the Valid state.

Device change / migration. Migration is a transition rather than a persisting state. A Wallet User moving to a new device establishes a new Wallet Unit on that device, which begins its own lifecycle at the Installed state; device-bound credentials are re-issued rather than copied, because device-bound keys cannot leave the device that created them. The source Wallet Unit is revoked once the transfer is complete. Migration is governed by clause 10.

Uninstalled. The Wallet Instance has been removed from the device and all key material, credentials and personal data have been irrecoverably deleted. This is a terminal state; a Wallet Unit does not return from it. Uninstallation is governed by clause 11 and results in deregistration and revocation of the Wallet Unit.

Revoked. The Wallet Unit has been permanently invalidated and can no longer be used; its status is published so that relying parties reject it. Revocation is permanent and irreversible, with no reactivation. This is a terminal state, entered from any active state on the grounds set out in clause 12, including breach detection, a legal requirement, a Wallet User request, and the revocation of a source Wallet Unit after migration.

Suspension and reactivation are not part of this lifecycle model: a Wallet Unit that can no longer be trusted is revoked, and recovery is achieved by activating a new Wallet Unit and re-issuing credentials.
